Chapter 01 · A practical study guide

Hello, world of concurrency in C++!

A chapter-one field guide to what concurrency means, when it helps, and the small C++11 program that launches a worker thread—and waits for it safely.

Anthony Williams C++ Concurrency in Action Chapter 1 · printed pages 1–14
The chapter's thesis
Starting threads is easy.
Designing them well is the work.
Use concurrency for a reasonDesign · Measure · Coordinate
What it isIndependent work making progress at once
Why use itClearer responsibilities or more throughput
What to watchOverhead, shared state, and coordination
01 / 05
The execution model

Concurrency is about progress, not a promise of speed.

A computer may interleave work on one core or run it truly in parallel on multiple hardware threads. Both are concurrent from the program's point of view; the performance and timing differ.

Core idea

Concurrency

Two or more independent activities make progress during overlapping periods. The operating system can switch between them, or the hardware can execute them at the same time.

Keep distinct

Task switching vs. hardware parallelism

One core takes turns between jobs; multiple cores can run separate jobs simultaneously. Switching has a cost, and a real machine may still switch when it has more runnable work than hardware capacity.

02 / 05
The “why”

Two good reasons. One important test.

Williams groups the motivation into separation of concerns and performance. If neither benefit is worth the added complexity, keep the work sequential.

↗

Separate responsibilities

Give distinct work its own flow—for example, keep a user interface responsive while another thread handles playback or background monitoring.

Design clarity
∥

Increase performance

Split different operations across workers (task parallelism) or apply the same operation to separate data chunks (data parallelism); independent items can also raise throughput.

Parallel work
!

Count the costs

Thread startup, context switches, limited resources, coordination, and harder testing can outweigh the gain—especially for tiny jobs.

Measure first

Chapter-one rule of thumb

Use concurrency where it produces a clear design benefit or a measurable performance gain.

More threads do not automatically mean more speed. Dependencies, contention, and oversubscription can erase the benefit or make the program slower.
03 / 05
Processes and threads

Isolation trades places with sharing.

The chapter uses the “separate offices vs. one shared office” analogy: separate processes isolate their data; threads in one process can reach shared data directly.

AspectMultiple processesMultiple threads in one process
MemoryUsually separate address spaces, with stronger protection between processes.Share an address space; data can often be passed or accessed directly.
CommunicationUses mechanisms such as pipes, sockets, signals, or files; setup and exchange can be heavier.Shared memory is lightweight, but shared data must be coordinated safely.
Main trade-offMore isolation and the option to distribute work across machines, at the cost of process and communication overhead.Lower overhead and direct sharing, at the cost of race risks and responsibility for consistent access.
iScope of this book: the chapter notes that C++ has no standard process-management interface, so the book focuses on threads and the C++ Standard Thread Library.

05 / 05
The first C++ example

One function, one worker, one join.

The book compares a single-threaded greeting with a C++11 version that starts a new thread. The example is intentionally tiny: it teaches the shape of the API, not a worthwhile optimization.

Sequential baseline
opening example · p. 13
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::cout << "Hello World\n";
}
A direct baseline: main() writes the message itself.
Concurrent version
Listing 1.1 · p. 13
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

void hello()
{
    std::cout << "Hello Concurrent World\n";
}

int main()
{
    std::thread worker(hello);
    worker.join();
}
std::thread starts hello(); join() makes main wait for that worker to finish.
Before C++11No standard thread-aware memory model; portable programs often relied on platform APIs or library wrappers.
→
C++11 and the standard libraryA thread-aware memory model, standard thread management, shared-data protection, synchronization, and atomic operations.
↗Build the example: save the concurrent listing as hello.cpp, then compile with a C++11-capable compiler—for example, g++ -std=c++11 -pthread hello.cpp -o hello. The browser demo above illustrates scheduling; it does not compile or execute this C++ program.
✓Efficiency note: the standard thread library aims to provide portable facilities with low abstraction overhead. Profile your program and try the standard tools before reaching for platform-specific APIs.
Chapter 1 · the takeaway

Threads are a tool for structure and throughput—not a goal by themselves.

Modern C++ makes creating a thread portable. The harder part is deciding what should run concurrently, what data it shares, and how the overall program stays correct.

  • Concurrency can mean interleaving or true parallel execution.
  • Threads share memory; processes provide stronger isolation.
  • Choose concurrency for separation of concerns or measured performance.
  • Account for startup cost, switching, resource limits, and coordination.

Quick recall

Try answering first, then open each note.

What is the difference between task switching and hardware concurrency?

Task switching shares one execution resource over time; hardware concurrency means separate hardware threads can make progress simultaneously.

What are the chapter's two main reasons to use concurrency?

Separation of concerns and performance: clearer independent responsibilities, or more work completed / more throughput.

Why can threads be cheaper than processes—and riskier?

Threads in one process share an address space and can communicate directly, but the programmer must protect shared state and keep each thread's view consistent.

What does join() do in the opening example?

It blocks the calling thread (main) until the associated worker thread has completed, preventing the program from ending too soon.

CH. 02
Next chapter · printed pages 15–32

Managing threads: make ownership explicit.

Chapter 2 turns the first std::thread into practical rules for starting, waiting, detaching, passing arguments, transferring ownership, choosing a worker count, and identifying a thread. The key safety rule: never let a joinable thread object be destroyed.

Start · then decide

Constructing std::thread starts the work.

Every new thread needs a callable entry point. Before its handle is destroyed, explicitly call join() or detach(); otherwise the thread object's destructor calls std::terminate().

Protect lifetime

Prefer scoped, exception-safe cleanup.

join() waits and releases the association. detach() gives up direct control while work continues in the background. Use RAII when a thread must finish before local data goes away—even on an exception path.

Thread-handle lifecycleOriginal study diagram · Chapter 2 uses code listings, not numbered figures
↳

Arguments have lifetime rules

The constructor stores argument values for the new thread. Wrap an intentional reference with std::ref; make sure the referenced object outlives the worker. Use std::move for move-only inputs.

Copy · reference · move
⇄

Thread handles move, not copy

A move transfers responsibility to another std::thread. The moved-from object no longer represents that worker. Never overwrite a still-joinable handle: replacing it would terminate the program.

Single owner
#

Size and identify deliberately

hardware_concurrency() is only a hint and can return zero. Bound workers by both hardware and useful work; use get_id() or this_thread::get_id() for logging or thread-specific behavior.

Avoid oversubscription

Parallel work is usually divided into blocks.

The chapter's parallel accumulate example splits a range, launches workers for some blocks, lets the calling thread handle another, then joins and combines partial results.

Its minimum block size avoids creating threads for tiny amounts of work. The example is illustrative, not production-ready: exception handling, floating-point grouping, and iterator requirements all need consideration.
02.1
Short C++ patterns

Make the rules visible in code.

These concise excerpts highlight the chapter's practical patterns. The example below using std::ref is a small standalone adaptation of the book's argument-passing discussion.

RAII join guard
Listing 2.3 · p. 20
#include <thread>

class thread_guard
{
    std::thread& t;
public:
    explicit thread_guard(std::thread& t_) : t(t_) {}
    ~thread_guard()
    {
        if (t.joinable()) t.join();
    }
    thread_guard(thread_guard const&) = delete;
    thread_guard& operator=(thread_guard const&) = delete;
};
The guard joins at scope exit, including exception paths. Declare it after the thread it references so it is destroyed first.
Pass a reference intentionally
§ 2.2 · p. 24
#include <functional>
#include <thread>

void increment(int& value) { ++value; }

int main()
{
    int value = 0;
    std::thread worker(increment, std::ref(value));
    worker.join();
    return value != 1;
}
Arguments are copied by default; std::ref opts into reference semantics. Joining keeps value alive until the update completes.
Transfer ownership
§ 2.3 · pp. 25–27
#include <thread>
#include <utility>

void do_work();

void transfer_and_join()
{
    std::thread original(do_work);
    std::thread owner = std::move(original);
    owner.join();
}
Moving a named handle explicitly transfers its thread. do_work() is defined elsewhere; the new owner must join or detach.
Hardware hint + current ID
§§ 2.4–2.5 · pp. 28, 31
#include <thread>

unsigned worker_hint()
{
    unsigned n = std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    return n == 0 ? 2 : n; // choose a fallback policy
}

std::thread::id current_thread_id()
{
    return std::this_thread::get_id();
}
hardware_concurrency() may return zero; cap any hint by the amount of useful work. Thread IDs are for identification, not portable semantic labels.
iDetached-thread caution: after detach(), the original handle cannot wait for that worker or regain ownership. Any pointers, references, or other resources it uses must remain valid until the detached work ends.

Chapter 2 quick recall

Try to answer before opening each note.

What must happen before a std::thread object is destroyed?

If it is joinable, either join it or detach it first. Otherwise its destructor calls std::terminate().

When is detach() a safe choice?

Only when the worker can safely outlive its handle and all data/resources it accesses will remain valid; detaching removes the ability to join it later.

How does std::thread pass arguments by default?

It stores copies of the supplied values. Use std::ref for a deliberate reference, with a lifetime that extends until the worker is done.

What does hardware_concurrency() guarantee?

It is only a hint about concurrent hardware execution, and may return zero. Bound thread count by both available work and a sensible hardware-based limit.

CH. 03
Next chapter · printed pages 33–66

Sharing data safely means preserving invariants.

Shared memory makes threads convenient, but simultaneous updates can expose half-finished changes. Chapter 3 builds a practical discipline around invariants, mutexes, interface design, lock ordering, and choosing a protection mechanism that fits the data.

↯

Understand the race

Read-only sharing is simplest. A race condition is an order-dependent outcome; it becomes problematic when ordering breaks an invariant. The C++ term data race is narrower and entails undefined behavior. Timing-sensitive failures can be hard to reproduce.

Invariants first
▣

Protect the whole operation

A mutex should cover the complete state transition that must appear indivisible—not just individual fields. Keep the protected data behind the lock; don't leak pointers or references through returns or callbacks.

Encapsulate shared state
↻

Locks create their own risks

Inconsistent lock order can deadlock. Locks held too long create contention; locks held too briefly can expose broken invariants. Use lock ordering and minimize critical-section work.

Correctness · then contention

Thread safety is also an interface-design problem.

Even individually locked methods can compose into an unsafe multi-step operation.

For example, if (!stack.empty()) { top(); pop(); } is not atomic: another consumer can change the stack between calls. Expose one operation that checks, retrieves, and removes under the same lock; choose a return strategy that also handles exceptions safely.
03.1
Practical protection patterns

Use RAII, deadlock-aware locking, and short critical sections.

These short C++ examples summarize the chapter's most reusable tools. Each code block can be copied independently.

Lock shared data with RAII
Listing 3.1 · p. 38
#include <list>
#include <mutex>

std::list<int> items;
std::mutex items_mutex;

void add_item(int value)
{
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(items_mutex);
    items.push_back(value);
}
std::lock_guard locks on construction and unlocks on every exit path, including exceptions.
Lock two mutexes together
§ 3.2.4 · p. 48
#include <mutex>
#include <utility>

std::mutex left_mutex, right_mutex;
int left_value = 0, right_value = 0;

void swap_values()
{
    std::lock(left_mutex, right_mutex);
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> left(
        left_mutex, std::adopt_lock);
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> right(
        right_mutex, std::adopt_lock);
    std::swap(left_value, right_value);
}
std::lock acquires both without deadlock; the guards adopt those locks and release them via RAII.
Release a lock while computing
§ 3.2.8 · p. 57
#include <mutex>

std::mutex m;
int shared_input = 0;
int shared_result = 0;
int expensive_process(int);

void process_input()
{
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(m);
    const int local = shared_input;
    lock.unlock();
    const int result = expensive_process(local);
    lock.lock();
    shared_result = result;
}
Use unique_lock for early unlock/relock or ownership transfer; prefer lock_guard when fixed-scope ownership is enough. Preserve the operation's meaning when shortening the lock.
Initialize exactly once
Listing 3.11 · p. 61
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>

struct Resource {};
std::once_flag init_flag;
std::shared_ptr<Resource> resource;

void init_resource()
{
    resource = std::make_shared<Resource>();
}
void use_resource()
{
    std::call_once(init_flag, init_resource);
}
std::call_once safely coordinates one-time initialization. C++11 also makes function-local static initialization thread-safe.
R

Read-mostly data

A reader-writer lock permits concurrent readers but exclusive writers. The 2012 chapter demonstrates boost::shared_mutex; profile the target workload before accepting the extra complexity.

Use when reads dominate
1×

One-time setup

Prefer std::call_once or C++11's thread-safe local-static initialization to a hand-rolled double-check outside a mutex.

Avoid double-checked locking
↺

Use recursive locks sparingly

std::recursive_mutex allows the same thread to lock again, but often hides tangled calls. A private helper that assumes the lock is already held is usually clearer.

Prefer a simpler design
!Deadlock checklist: avoid nested locks where possible; don't call unknown/user-supplied code while holding a lock; if several locks are necessary, use std::lock or a consistent global order. Avoid waiting for another thread while holding a lock it may need.

Chapter 3 quick recall

Try to answer before opening each note.

What is an invariant, and how can a race break it?

An invariant is a property that should hold for a data structure. A multi-step update can temporarily break it; another thread must not observe or act on that intermediate state.

Why prefer lock_guard to manual lock()/unlock()?

RAII ensures the mutex is released on every exit path, including exceptions. Use unique_lock only when its extra flexibility—deferred locking, early unlock, or ownership transfer—is needed.

Can individually thread-safe methods still make an unsafe sequence?

Yes. Separate empty(), top(), and pop() calls can interleave. Design one operation that protects the full logical transition.

What are the basic deadlock-avoidance habits?

Avoid nested locks and callbacks under locks; acquire multiple locks together with std::lock or in a consistent order; don't wait for a thread while holding a lock it may need.

How do call_once and reader-writer locks help?

call_once coordinates one-time setup. A reader-writer lock can allow simultaneous readers and an exclusive writer when reads dominate, but should be justified by profiling.

CHAPTER
04
Synchronizing concurrent operations · printed pp. 67–102

Let threads wait for events—not guesses.

Chapter 3 was about protecting shared data. Here the focus shifts to coordinating work: block efficiently until a condition is true, pass one-time results between tasks, put a bound on waiting, and choose designs that need less shared state.

4.1Condition variables 4.2Futures & promises 4.3Deadlines & clocks 4.4Functional & messages 4.5Summary & recall
4.1
Wait for a condition

Sleep until work arrives; don't poll for it.

A condition variable lets a thread block until shared state may have changed. The condition itself lives in ordinary shared data, protected by a mutex; the condition variable is the wake-up mechanism.

The wait protocol

Lock · test · wait · test again

Call wait with a std::unique_lock and a predicate. If it is false, the wait atomically releases the mutex and blocks; after a wake-up it reacquires the mutex and checks the predicate again.

The state is the truth

Notifications aren't stored events

Push a job into the mutex-protected queue, then notify. If nobody is waiting, the queued item is still there; the next consumer sees the true predicate before it ever blocks.

! Why the predicate matters: wake-ups can be spurious, and several consumers may race for the same item. wait(lock, predicate) is effectively a loop that re-checks the predicate while holding the mutex. Use notify_one() when one worker should claim new work; use notify_all() when every waiter needs a chance to re-check shared state.
PATTERN
A thread-safe queue

Make waiting and removing one operation.

A consumer should not separately check empty(), read front(), and call pop(); another thread could change the queue between those calls. A blocking wait_and_pop() and a nonblocking try_pop() provide a safer, useful interface.

Wait safely for a queue item
§ 4.1 · pp. 72–75
#include <condition_variable>
#include <mutex>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>

template<class T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
    std::mutex mutex_;
    std::condition_variable ready_;
    std::queue<T> queue_;
public:
    void push(T value)
    {
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
            queue_.push(std::move(value));
        }
        ready_.notify_one();
    }

    void wait_and_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        ready_.wait(lock, [this] { return !queue_.empty(); });
        value = std::move(queue_.front());
        queue_.pop();
    }

    bool try_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        if (queue_.empty()) return false;
        value = std::move(queue_.front());
        queue_.pop();
        return true;
    }
};
One lock, one logical operation. The condition and queue share a mutex; notify after publishing the item. The consumer releases the lock when wait_and_pop returns, before doing slower work.
Choosing the operation

wait_and_pop or try_pop?

wait_and_pop blocks efficiently until the queue is non-empty, then removes an item while holding the queue's lock. try_pop returns immediately with success/failure. Neither asks callers to split a check from the removal.

std::condition_variable works with std::mutex; condition_variable_any accepts other lockable types but may cost more. For a general-purpose queue, also decide how shutdown is signaled, how values are returned, and what happens if moving a value throws.

4.2
One-off events

Use futures to carry a result to its reader.

A future represents an asynchronous result that becomes ready once. A task can finish with a value or an exception; a waiting thread can do other work first, then collect the outcome with get().

One result · one reader

std::future<T>

Move-only ownership of a shared result. wait() blocks without retrieving it; get() waits if needed, returns the value (or rethrows the stored exception), and consumes the future's result.

One result · many readers

std::shared_future<T>

Copyable handles let several threads wait for and read the same result. Give each thread its own copy; concurrently calling members on one shared-future object still needs synchronization.

A

std::async

Conveniently launches a callable and returns a future for its result. With the default policy, the implementation may choose asynchronous or deferred execution.

Task + result
T

std::packaged_task

Wraps a callable and its signature in a movable task. Obtain its future, then let a thread, queue, or scheduler decide when to invoke it.

Callable + future
P

std::promise

Manually fulfills a future with set_value or set_exception. Useful when completion comes from an event, I/O operation, or another control path.

Explicit result source
Launch a calculation with std::async
Listing 4.6 · p. 77
#include <future>

int compute_answer() { return 42; }
void do_other_work() {}

int main()
{
    std::future<int> answer =
        std::async(std::launch::async, compute_answer);
    do_other_work();
    return answer.get() == 42 ? 0 : 1;
}
get() is the synchronization point. This example explicitly requests asynchronous execution. Without a launch policy, C++11 permits deferred execution as well as asynchronous execution.
Bind a task to a future
§ 4.2.2 · p. 79
#include <future>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>

int main()
{
    std::packaged_task<int(int)> task(
        [](int n) { return n * n; });
    std::future<int> result = task.get_future();
    std::thread worker(std::move(task), 7);
    worker.join();
    return result.get() == 49 ? 0 : 1;
}
The task packages the result, not the scheduler. Here a thread invokes it; a pool could instead take the packaged task from a work queue. Exceptions from the callable are stored for get().
Fulfill a promise from a worker
§ 4.2.3 · pp. 81–83
#include <exception>
#include <future>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>

int calculate() { return 6 * 7; }
void produce(std::promise<int> promise)
{
    try { promise.set_value(calculate()); }
    catch (...) {
        promise.set_exception(std::current_exception());
    }
}
int main()
{
    std::promise<int> promise;
    std::future<int> result = promise.get_future();
    std::thread worker(produce, std::move(promise));
    worker.join();
    return result.get() == 42 ? 0 : 1;
}
The producer owns the promise. If a promise or packaged task is abandoned before publishing a result, the future becomes ready with broken_promise instead of waiting forever.
↗ Errors travel with the result: an exception thrown by an async callable or packaged task is stored and rethrown by get(). A promise can explicitly store an exception. Always decide who owns the future, who calls get(), and how the task's lifetime is joined or otherwise managed.
4.3
Bounded waits

Use a clock that matches the question.

Waiting indefinitely is not always acceptable. The standard library offers duration-based _for waits and absolute _until deadlines for futures, condition variables, sleeps, and timed mutexes.

How long?wait_for(250 ms) · a duration
↔
Until when?wait_until(deadline) · a time point
Measure elapsed time

steady_clock

Monotonic and not adjusted to match wall time. Prefer it for timeouts, elapsed intervals, and a deadline computed as “now plus a budget.”

Schedule by civil time

system_clock

Represents the system's wall clock, which can be corrected or changed. Use it for calendar-style times, not for measuring a guaranteed elapsed interval.

Wait until one steady deadline
Listing 4.11 · p. 91
#include <chrono>
#include <condition_variable>
#include <mutex>

std::condition_variable changed;
std::mutex mutex;
bool done = false;

bool wait_for_done()
{
    const auto deadline = std::chrono::steady_clock::now()
        + std::chrono::milliseconds(500);
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mutex);
    while (!done) {
        if (changed.wait_until(lock, deadline)
                == std::cv_status::timeout)
            break;
    }
    return done;
}
Compute the deadline once. Repeating a fresh wait_for(500ms) after each spurious wake can extend the total wait indefinitely. A single steady-clock deadline bounds the whole loop.
Check the status

Timeout is not cancellation.

A timed wait reports whether the event arrived before the limit; it doesn't stop the work. A future wait can also report ready, timeout, or deferred. A timeout is a prompt to choose what the caller should do next.

std::chrono::duration stores a count and unit; a time_point belongs to a clock. Converting to a coarser duration with duration_cast truncates. Condition-variable predicate overloads, sleep_for/sleep_until, and timed-mutex try_lock_for/try_lock_until cover common wait policies.

4.4
Make synchronization disappear

Pass results or messages instead of sharing mutable state.

Condition variables and futures are building blocks. A higher-level design can make the synchronization boundary explicit—or avoid shared mutation altogether.

Functional-style concurrency

Inputs in · result out

A pure function depends only on its arguments and doesn't mutate external state. Independent calls can run concurrently; futures carry each result to the task that needs it.

Message passing

Actors own their state

Each actor handles messages on its own thread and owns its local state. A mailbox or message library coordinates delivery, so the application reasons about messages and state transitions rather than every lock.

i Neither is magic: functional-style tasks still need careful task sizing and scheduling; spawning work recursively can oversubscribe a machine. Message-passing systems still need reliable queues, shutdown rules, and clear message ownership. The win is a smaller shared-state surface and a more explicit flow of work.

Choose the shape that fits

Use futures for one-off dependencies and return values; use an actor/message boundary when ongoing interactions and ownership of state matter.

The chapter's ATM sketch runs its logic as a state machine: wait for the messages valid in the current state, handle one, then transition. A real C++ program needs a mailbox implementation; the standard library does not provide a general message-passing framework.
4.5 · Chapter summary

Coordinate at the boundary of the work.

Condition variables coordinate predicates; futures coordinate one-time results. Deadlines bound waits. Functional-style tasks and message passing can reduce the amount of shared mutable state that must be protected.

  • Guard the condition with a mutex; wait with a predicate and re-check after every wake-up.
  • Use futures to carry values or exceptions; share copies when multiple readers need one result.
  • Use one steady-clock deadline for an elapsed-time budget; a timeout does not cancel work.
  • Prefer clear result flow or message ownership to ad hoc shared-state coordination.

Chapter 4 quick recall

Try to answer before opening each note.

Why should a condition-variable wait use a predicate?

Wake-ups can be spurious, and another thread may consume the condition first. The predicate is re-checked while the mutex is held; the wait blocks only while it is false.

Why combine waiting and popping in a queue?

Checking empty(), reading front(), and popping in separate calls leaves gaps where another consumer can change the queue. wait_and_pop() makes the logical removal one protected operation.

What is the difference between async, packaged_task, and promise?

async launches a callable and returns its future; packaged_task binds a callable to a future but leaves scheduling to its owner; promise lets a producer explicitly set a value or exception.

When should you use shared_future?

When several threads need the same one-time result. Copy the shared_future so each thread uses its own handle; do not concurrently call members on one shared_future object without synchronization.

Which clock is usually right for a timeout?

steady_clock, because it is monotonic. Compute one absolute deadline for the full wait loop; use system_clock for wall-clock schedules that refer to civil time.

How do futures and message passing simplify synchronization?

Futures make result dependencies explicit; message passing gives each actor ownership of its state and communicates through messages. Both can reduce direct sharing of mutable data.

CHAPTER
05
The C++ memory model · printed pp. 103–147

Know what your atomics order—and what they don't.

Mutexes and futures hide most memory-model details. When code uses atomics directly, correctness depends on the exact relationship between accesses: which data races are undefined, which operations synchronize, and what each memory-order tag guarantees.

5.1Objects & memory locations 5.2Atomic types & operations 5.3Happens-before & ordering 5.4Summary & recall
5.1
The structural rules

Reason about memory locations, not just variable names.

C++ describes program data as objects occupying memory locations. Most scalar objects have their own location; adjacent bit-fields can share one. Whether concurrent accesses conflict is defined at that level.

The dangerous case

A data race is undefined behavior.

Conflicting, unsynchronized accesses to one memory location—at least one a non-atomic write—form a data race. A data race is not merely a stale value: the C++ program has undefined behavior.

Atomic doesn't mean ordered

Atomicity and synchronization are separate.

Atomic operations cannot be observed half-complete and avoid a data race on that atomic object. But a relaxed atomic flag alone does not publish unrelated data or order accesses to other objects.

→ One modification order per object: all threads agree on the order of modifications to a given atomic object. That does not by itself create one global order across different objects. Use a mutex or an explicit atomic synchronization relationship when another thread must observe a coordinated set of changes.
5.2
The standard atomic types

Atomic operations are indivisible; lock-free is a different promise.

The specializations in <atomic> provide atomic access to values. They are not copyable like ordinary variables, and most are not required to be lock-free: an implementation may use an internal lock.

A

std::atomic<T>

Core operations include load, store, exchange, and compare/exchange. Eligible trivially-copyable types can use the primary template; it does not make a whole container atomic.

One object · one operation
↻

Read–modify–write

Integral atomics add operations such as fetch_add and fetch_or; pointer atomics support atomic pointer arithmetic. A read–modify–write observes and updates one atomic object as one operation.

Counter · flag · pointer
⇄

Compare / exchange

Update only if the current value matches expected. On failure, expected is overwritten with the value actually observed. The weak form may fail spuriously, so use it in a retry loop.

CAS retry loop
≠

Atomic is not lock-free

std::atomic_flag is guaranteed lock-free. Other atomic types may report is_lock_free() == false; even lock-free code can still contend or waste CPU.

Check the implementation
Count independent events
§ 5.2 · pp. 107–110
#include <atomic>

std::atomic<unsigned long long> events(0);

void record_event()
{
    events.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
}
A relaxed atomic counter is suitable when the count itself must be indivisible but it does not publish or protect other data. The relaxed tag provides no cross-object ordering.
Retry a compare/exchange update
§ 5.2.3 · p. 113
#include <atomic>

std::atomic<int> best(0);

void publish_max(int candidate)
{
    int current = best.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    while (current < candidate &&
           !best.compare_exchange_weak(
               current, candidate,
               std::memory_order_relaxed,
               std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
        // On failure, current is refreshed; retry.
    }
}
Weak CAS belongs in a loop. Contention can change the value; a spurious failure can also ask for a retry even when the value matched. The failed call refreshes current.
A minimal atomic_flag spin lock
Listing 5.1 · pp. 111–112
#include <atomic>
#include <mutex>

class spinlock_mutex
{
    std::atomic_flag flag;
public:
    spinlock_mutex() : flag(ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT) {}

    void lock()
    {
        while (flag.test_and_set(
                   std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
    }
    void unlock()
    {
        flag.clear(std::memory_order_release);
    }
};

spinlock_mutex guard;
void update()
{
    std::lock_guard<spinlock_mutex> lock(guard);
    // protected work
}
Study example, not a default mutex. The lock spins while busy, consuming CPU. A regular std::mutex is usually the better choice when contention or waiting is possible.
More than the core template

Pick the type for the operation.

Atomic integral and pointer specializations have additional arithmetic and bitwise operations. C++11 also provides free std::atomic_* functions, including atomic access to std::shared_ptr.

Use a mutex for multi-step invariants or rich objects. The fact that one field is atomic does not make a larger data structure or algorithm atomic.

! Do not infer progress guarantees from the type name. Atomicity means an operation is indivisible. Lock-free means the implementation meets a stronger progress property; it is not guaranteed for most std::atomic<T> specializations, and it does not mean wait-free or contention-free.
5.3
Synchronizing operations

Build a happens-before path from the writer to the reader.

Within a thread, operations are sequenced. Across threads, a synchronizes-with edge—such as a release store observed by an acquire load—can connect those operations. Transitivity then gives a happens-before relationship for the data that must be visible.

Within one threadsequenced-before

Earlier operations establish the local part of the chain.

→
Across threadssynchronizes-with

A release operation pairs with an acquire that observes its value.

→
By transitivityhappens-before

Writes before release become visible to reads after acquire.

↗ Publication example: write ordinary data, then store true to an atomic flag with release semantics. If another thread's acquire load observes that store, the ordinary write happens-before the reader's later access. The payload itself need not be atomic in this one-writer/one-publication pattern.
Publish ordinary data with release/acquire
Listing 5.2 · p. 120
#include <atomic>
#include <cassert>
#include <thread>

int payload = 0;
std::atomic<bool> ready(false);

void writer()
{
    payload = 42;
    ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
}
void reader()
{
    while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
    assert(payload == 42);
}
int main()
{
    std::thread producer(writer);
    reader();
    producer.join();
}
The acquire must observe the release publication. This low-level spin is for illustrating the ordering; prefer a condition variable or future when a thread should block efficiently.
ORDERS
The memory-order tags

Start with the strongest order; weaken only with a proof.

Unless a different order is specified, atomic operations use memory_order_seq_cst. The other orders trade a simpler global model for narrower guarantees.

OrderGuaranteeGood mental model
seq_cstSequentially consistent atomics participate in one total order, consistent with each thread's sequencing.The easiest model to reason about; the default. Use it until measurement and a proof justify something narrower.
acquire / releaseA release store synchronizes with an acquire load that reads from it (or its release sequence); preceding writes become visible after the acquire.Pairwise publication, not one global order. Use acq_rel for a read–modify–write that needs both sides.
relaxedOperations remain atomic and each object retains a modification order, but relaxed operations alone create no synchronizes-with edge.Useful for independent counters and flags when no other state is being published. Different atomics may appear in different orders.
consumeA specialized dependency-ordering mode from the C++11 model; it is difficult to use portably and correctly.Prefer acquire unless you are deliberately engineering and verifying a dependency chain.
i Operation matters: stores can use release, loads can use acquire, and read–modify–write operations can use acquire, release, or both. The release part of a failed compare/exchange is not performed, so its failure order cannot be release or acquire–release.
TRY IT
Interactive memory-model demo

Can the reader see y == true and x == false?

Choose an ordering for a writer that stores x then y, and a reader that waits for y before loading x. Try a particular outcome and see whether the model permits it.

Two atomic variables · one writer · one reader

Allowed outcomes

Assume x and y start false, and the reader's load of y observes the writer's store of true. The demo is a model of permitted outcomes, not a simulation of a particular CPU.

Writer · in order
x.store(true, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
y.store(true, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
Reader · after observing y
while (!y.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst)) {}
bool observed_x = x.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst);
With sequential consistency, the reader observes one total order of all these atomic operations.

For release/acquire, the example assumes the acquire load reads the release store. With relaxed ordering, both flags are still atomic, but seeing y does not publish x.

Release sequences

Read–modify–write chains can carry publication forward.

A release store followed by a qualifying chain of atomic read–modify–write operations can synchronize with a later acquire that observes the sequence. That can let multiple consumers safely see data published before the original release, without making every consumer release to every other consumer.

Fences

Ordering barriers need an atomic communication point.

atomic_thread_fence can constrain surrounding atomic operations and thereby order nearby non-atomic accesses. A fence alone does not communicate; its pairing rules are subtle, so prefer direct acquire/release operations unless a measured design needs fences.

! Low-level ordering has a reasoning cost. Relaxed, acquire/release, consume, release sequences, and fences are not interchangeable performance knobs. Prove which operation reads which value, draw the happens-before edges, and test on every target; otherwise keep the default sequentially consistent order or use a higher-level primitive.
5.4 · Chapter summary

Atomicity protects one operation. Ordering connects operations.

The memory model defines when conflicting accesses are valid and how one thread can make its earlier work visible to another. Atomics are precise low-level tools—not automatic substitutes for a mutex or a sound ownership design.

  • A data race on a non-atomic memory location is undefined behavior; bit-fields can share a memory location.
  • Each atomic object has a modification order, but relaxed operations do not create a cross-object publication edge.
  • Release/acquire can publish prior writes when the acquire observes the release; happens-before is transitive.
  • Sequential consistency is the easiest global model and the default; weaken it only when correctness is proved and measurement warrants it.

Chapter 5 quick recall

Try to answer before opening each note.

What makes a C++ data race undefined behavior?

Conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory location, where at least one access is a non-atomic write. Separate ordinary scalar objects are separate memory locations; adjacent bit-fields may not be.

Does an atomic operation automatically publish other data?

No. Atomicity applies to that atomic object's operation. A relaxed flag does not order unrelated payload accesses; use a matching release/acquire pair or another synchronization mechanism.

What does happens-before tell you?

It connects sequenced operations within a thread to synchronizing operations across threads. By transitivity, writes before a release can happen-before reads after an acquire that observes it.

When is relaxed ordering appropriate?

When the atomic value itself needs atomic access but its operations do not need to publish or order other data—for example, an independent event counter.

What changes when you use compare_exchange_weak?

It may fail spuriously. On failure, expected is refreshed with the value observed, so the usual pattern retries in a loop and recalculates from that value.

Why is sequential consistency the recommended starting point?

It gives sequentially consistent atomic operations one total order and is the default, making outcomes easier to reason about. Weaker orders require a precise proof of the needed synchronization.

CHAPTER
06
Lock-based concurrent data structures · printed pp. 148–179

Treat the interface, invariants, and lock scope as one design.

A mutex can prevent races, but a data structure is only useful when its operations are safe as a whole—and its locking leaves room for independent work to proceed concurrently.

6.1Design for concurrency 6.2Stacks & queues 6.2.3Fine-grained queue 6.3Tables & lists 6.4Summary & recall
6.1
Two goals, not one

Safety preserves the invariants; design creates opportunities to overlap work.

A thread-safe data structure gives every supported concurrent operation a self-consistent view: invariants hold, items are not lost or corrupted, and accesses do not race. Which combinations of operations are supported is part of its contract.

Correctness first

Guard complete state transitions.

Identify the invariants and protect every read or write that participates in them. Design operations around the real task—such as “remove and return one item”—rather than exposing separately locked steps that callers must combine.

Throughput next

Keep unrelated work independent.

A single mutex is often the clearest safe starting point, but it serializes every operation using it. Once correctness is established, ask whether distinct regions can have distinct locks and whether allocation or cleanup can happen outside a critical section.

01
Make the interface race-resistant

Do not make callers test, inspect, and then modify state in separate calls. Put the check and its action inside one operation.

02
Plan for exceptions

Choose a commit point. If transferring a value can throw, do it before unlinking the item—or document the guarantees required of the value type.

03
Constrain lock lifetime and order

Use RAII, keep critical sections short, avoid calling unknown code while locked when possible, and define one order for nested locks.

04
Make lifetime a user-visible rule

Construction and destruction require exclusive access. Publish an initialized object safely, document copy/assignment/swap constraints, and stop every worker before destruction.

↗ More locks do not automatically mean more concurrency. Every shared pointer, link, size, and invariant still needs a protection plan. A finer-grained design is worthwhile only when its lock boundaries match genuinely independent parts of the data structure.
6.2
Small interfaces, strong guarantees

Combine the check with the action; make waiting part of the queue.

The stack and condition-variable queue from earlier chapters illustrate two recurring design rules: make a pop one indivisible operation, and let a condition variable wait on a predicate instead of polling an empty check.

Split calls leave a race window
empty()→top()→pop()

Even if each method takes a lock, another thread can remove the item between calls. The sequence is not one atomic operation.

One call owns the transition
try_pop()orwait_and_pop()

Check for data, select it, and remove it under the same synchronization. Return the value—or a smart pointer—or report that the queue was empty.

↔

Choose the empty-case contract

A nonblocking pop can return a success flag or an empty smart pointer. A blocking pop can wait on !queue.empty() with a unique_lock; the condition-variable wait releases and reacquires that lock around sleep.

Predicate · not polling
!

Do not lose an item on failure

Construct or transfer the result before unlinking the node when that step may throw. Returning a shared_ptr can make the post-removal handoff non-throwing; guarantees still depend on the value type's copy/move behavior.

Exception-safe commit point
⏱

Move slow work out of the lock

For a queue of smart pointers, prepare the payload before locking, enqueue the pointer, release the lock, and then notify a waiter. Allocation and notification need not lengthen the protected link update.

Short critical section
↗

State what callers may do

References and iterators can outlive the lock or point to an erased item. Prefer values, smart pointers, snapshots, and a documented list of operations that may safely overlap.

Contract is part of safety
Stack · one safe pop operation
Listing 6.1 · pp. 151–152
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <stack>
#include <utility>

template<typename T>
class safe_stack
{
    std::stack<T> data_;
    mutable std::mutex mutex_;

public:
    void push(T value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        data_.push(std::move(value));
    }

    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        if (data_.empty())
            return std::shared_ptr<T>();

        std::shared_ptr<T> result(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(data_.top())));
        data_.pop();
        return result;
    }
};
Single linearized step: the emptiness check, transfer, and removal share one lock. The returned pointer may be empty; there is no separate empty() → top() → pop() race.
Queue · wait on a predicate
Listing 6.3 · pp. 156–157
#include <condition_variable>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>

template<typename T>
class waiting_queue
{
    std::mutex mutex_;
    std::queue<std::shared_ptr<T> > data_;
    std::condition_variable ready_;

public:
    void push(T value)
    {
        auto item = std::make_shared<T>(std::move(value));
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
            data_.push(std::move(item));
        }
        ready_.notify_one();
    }

    std::shared_ptr<T> wait_and_pop()
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        ready_.wait(lock, [this] { return !data_.empty(); });
        auto result = data_.front();
        data_.pop();
        return result;
    }
};
Sleep, don't poll: the predicate is checked with the queue lock; wait() releases it while sleeping and reacquires it before returning. Preparing the payload before locking shortens the critical section.
i A lock can expose user code too. Copy/move constructors, assignments, predicates, and callbacks may run while a node is protected. They can lengthen contention or re-enter other locked code; keep them well behaved and do not let references escape the protected operation.
6.2.3
A linked queue with separate ends

A dummy node separates the head work from the tail work.

A plain singly linked queue has a subtle one-item case: head == tail, so a push and a pop can touch the same node's next pointer. Protecting head and tail with different mutexes is not enough if the two operations still share that link.

Separate the nodesKeep one empty dummy node.

The head and tail initially point to the dummy. A push fills the old tail and appends a fresh dummy; a pop advances the head. The dummy ensures the active head link and tail link are distinct.

Separate the locksProtect head and tail independently.

push() takes only tail_mutex. A pop takes head_mutex and briefly takes tail_mutex to test emptiness. The fixed head-then-tail lock order avoids a cycle.

Separate setup from commitAllocate before locking.

Build the payload and new dummy node off-lock; under the tail lock, link them and advance tail. Return the removed payload and destroy its old node after releasing the head lock.

C++11 fine-grained queue core
Listing 6.6 · pp. 161–162
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <utility>

template<typename T>
class fine_grained_queue
{
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::unique_ptr<node> next;
    };

    std::mutex head_mutex;
    std::unique_ptr<node> head;
    std::mutex tail_mutex;
    node* tail;

    node* get_tail()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(tail_mutex);
        return tail;
    }

    std::unique_ptr<node> pop_head()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(head_mutex);
        if (head.get() == get_tail())
            return std::unique_ptr<node>();

        std::unique_ptr<node> old_head = std::move(head);
        head = std::move(old_head->next);
        return old_head;
    }

public:
    fine_grained_queue() : head(new node), tail(head.get()) {}

    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> old_head = pop_head();
        return old_head ? old_head->data : std::shared_ptr<T>();
    }

    void push(T value)
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(value)));
        std::unique_ptr<node> new_node(new node);
        node* const new_tail = new_node.get();

        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(tail_mutex);
        tail->data = data;
        tail->next = std::move(new_node);
        tail = new_tail;
    }
};
Why the order matters: pop_head() keeps the head lock while it briefly snapshots the tail under the tail lock. That tail-lock handoff also orders the check against a push publishing data; the sole nested order is head then tail. This excerpt is nonblocking; the full queue adds predicate-based waiting on head != get_tail().
A legal interleaving

Different ends can progress together.

With queued data present, a pop can hold head_mutex while a push holds tail_mutex. The dummy node ensures those operations work on distinct nodes. This increases the opportunity for overlap; it does not guarantee speedup or eliminate contention.

For the blocking overload, wait on head != get_tail() while holding the head lock. Wake after the tail update and release its lock. For a bounded queue, producers also need a capacity predicate.

Interactive lock-scope lab

Can a push and pop overlap safely?

Ready

Assume the queue already holds several items, so its head and tail are separated by at least one real node. Step through one enqueue and one dequeue; this is an illustrative schedule, not a running concurrent program.

Producer · push(D)Ready
Consumer · pop(A)Ready
    Choose a lock layout, then advance the schedule.

    The fine-grained overlap relies on the dummy node and the queue being non-empty. Empty checks and other shared links still need synchronization.

    6.3
    More access patterns, more coordination

    Partition data by the operation that owns it.

    Lookup tables and linked lists have richer interfaces than a stack or queue. A useful locking plan follows their structure: select a hash bucket for a key, or hand a lock from one list node to the next.

    Hash table · one lock per bucket

    Route first, then lock the smallest relevant region.

    With a fixed bucket array, hash(key) % bucket_count chooses a bucket independently of other keys. A mutex per bucket lets operations on different buckets proceed at once; colliding keys still share that bucket's lock.

    hash(key)→bucket 0 · mutex 0
    hash(key)→bucket 1 · mutex 1
    hash(key)→bucket N−1 · mutex N−1
    Lookup table

    Return values, not unlocked iterators.

    Offer a small API—add/update, remove, and get a value or default. Returning references or iterators makes erasure and lifetime hard to synchronize. A whole-table snapshot locks every bucket in one consistent order; resizing also needs a coordinated plan.

    The 2012 example uses boost::shared_mutex for concurrent readers in one bucket. C++11 has no standard std::shared_mutex; a per-bucket std::mutex is the portable standard-library option.

    Linked list

    Hand the lock forward, node by node.

    A permanent sentinel lets push_front() update the first link under only the head lock. Traversal, search, update, and conditional removal use lock coupling: acquire the next node before releasing the current one. Removal is safe because no new traversal can reach an unlinked node while its predecessor stays locked.

    Iteration callbacks and predicates run under a node lock. They must not retain references beyond that lock or re-enter the list in a way that creates a lock cycle. Operations progress in list order; a slow callback can hold up followers.

    Bucket-local read / update
    Listing 6.11 · pp. 171–173
    #include <algorithm>
#include <list>
#include <mutex>
#include <utility>

template<typename Key, typename Value>
class bucket
{
    typedef std::pair<Key, Value> entry;
    std::list<entry> data_;
    mutable std::mutex mutex_;

public:
    Value value_for(Key const& key, Value const& fallback) const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        auto found = std::find_if(data_.begin(), data_.end(),
            [&](entry const& item) { return item.first == key; });
        return found == data_.end() ? fallback : found->second;
    }

    void add_or_update(Key const& key, Value const& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        auto found = std::find_if(data_.begin(), data_.end(),
            [&](entry const& item) { return item.first == key; });
        if (found == data_.end())
            data_.push_back(entry(key, value));
        else
            found->second = value;
    }
};
    One bucket at a time: the table hashes a key to a fixed bucket, then calls that bucket's operation. A mutex serializes access within this bucket; a shared mutex can allow multiple readers if the library provides one.
    Hand-over-hand traversal
    Listing 6.13 · pp. 176–177
    #include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <utility>

template<typename T>
class hand_over_hand_list
{
    struct node
    {
        std::mutex mutex;
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::unique_ptr<node> next;
        node() = default;
        explicit node(T const& value) : data(std::make_shared<T>(value)) {}
    };
    node head_;

public:
    void push_front(T const& value)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> new_node(new node(value));
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(head_.mutex);
        new_node->next = std::move(head_.next);
        head_.next = std::move(new_node);
    }

    template<typename Function>
    void for_each(Function f)
    {
        node* current = &head_;
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(head_.mutex);
        while (node* next = current->next.get())
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> next_lock(next->mutex);
            lock.unlock();
            f(*next->data);
            current = next;
            lock = std::move(next_lock);
        }
    }
};
    Move forward safely: while current is locked, its next link is stable. Acquire the next node before releasing the current one; the traversal can never overtake a slower operation ahead.
    ↕ Whole-container operations need a global plan. If ordinary calls take one bucket lock but a snapshot takes them all, acquire buckets in a single stable order every time. Lock-order consistency is what prevents the snapshot from deadlocking with another multi-lock operation.
    6.4 · Chapter summary

    First make the operation safe; then find independent regions.

    Lock-based structures are built from invariants, interfaces, and a deliberate lock topology. Coarse locking is a sound baseline; finer locking trades simplicity for more opportunity to overlap operations.

    • Document which operations may overlap, and expose complete actions rather than race-prone check-then-act steps.
    • Use RAII, plan exception guarantees and object lifetime, and keep lock order consistent.
    • A dummy node lets a linked queue protect head and tail separately; inspect the empty check and every shared link.
    • Bucket locks partition lookup-table updates; node locks enable list traversal, with callbacks and references kept within their contract.

    Chapter 6 quick recall

    Try to answer before opening each note.

    What makes a data structure thread-safe?

    For the documented combinations of concurrent operations, every thread sees a self-consistent state: invariants hold, data is not lost or corrupted, and there are no unsynchronized conflicting accesses.

    Why is a separately locked empty() check unsafe before pop()?

    Another thread can change the structure between the calls. Put the emptiness check and removal in one operation such as try_pop() or wait_and_pop().

    What does the dummy node fix in a fine-grained queue?

    It keeps the active head link and tail link on distinct nodes, avoiding the one-element case where push and pop would modify the same next pointer under different locks.

    Why must get_tail() run while the head lock is held?

    Otherwise another pop can advance head after the tail snapshot; the saved tail may no longer belong to the list, so a later comparison could corrupt the queue.

    How can a fixed-bucket hash table allow concurrent updates?

    Hash each key to a bucket and protect each bucket independently. Different buckets can proceed together; a full snapshot locks all buckets in a consistent order.

    What is lock coupling in a linked list?

    Acquire the next node's lock before releasing the current node's lock. This protects the link while moving forward and lets operations on separate nodes overlap.

    What limits a callback-based thread-safe list?

    The callback often executes while a node is locked. It must not leak references or re-enter other locked code unsafely; a slow callback also blocks traversals that reach that node.

    CHAPTER
    07
    Designing lock-free concurrent data structures · printed pp. 180–223

    A lock-free design is about progress and lifetime—not just replacing mutexes with atomics.

    Atomic operations can make individual pointer updates indivisible, but the algorithm must also guarantee useful progress, publish initialized nodes in the right order, and keep every node alive while another thread may still dereference it.

    7.1Progress guarantees 7.2.1Stack & compare/exchange 7.2.2–4Safe reclamation 7.2.5Memory ordering 7.2.6Queue & helping 7.3–4Guidelines & recall
    7.1
    Four different progress contracts

    “No mutex” is not the same thing as “lock-free.”

    Progress guarantees describe what the algorithm promises when threads interleave, stall, or contend. The names are precise: a busy loop can be nonblocking without being lock-free, and lock-free does not promise every individual thread will win.

    May suspend

    Blocking

    A thread waits for another action—such as a mutex unlock or condition-variable notification—before it can continue.

    No blocking call

    Nonblocking

    The algorithm avoids blocking library calls. It may still spin while another thread owns a resource or while its own compare/exchange keeps failing.

    System-wide progress

    Lock-free

    Ongoing contention cannot stop all operations: at least one operation completes in a finite number of steps. A particular thread may starve or retry indefinitely.

    Per-thread guarantee

    Wait-free

    Every thread completes its operation within a bounded number of its own steps, regardless of what other threads do. This is much harder to achieve.

    Why consider it?

    A paused participant need not hold the whole structure hostage.

    Lock-free algorithms avoid mutex deadlock and can tolerate a thread being suspended midway through an update. Wait-free algorithms add a stronger bound for every participant.

    What it costs

    More atomics do not automatically mean more speed.

    Retry loops can livelock or starve, shared cache lines can ping-pong, and allocation plus reclamation can dominate. Atomics for a composite value may use an internal lock on a given platform.

    ! Prove the progress property you need, then measure it. Check whether the actual atomic types are lock-free (for example, with is_lock_free()), compare against a mutex-based baseline, and measure the metric that matters to the application. A spinlock is nonblocking, but a stalled owner can prevent every other thread from entering, so it is not lock-free.
    7.2.1
    A stack: one atomic head

    Prepare a node privately; publish it with one compare/exchange.

    For push, construct the value and node completely before making the node reachable. Then try to replace head; if another thread changed it, compare/exchange refreshes the expected pointer and the operation retries with the new head.

    01 · PrepareConstruct the new node.

    No other thread can see it yet; finish its data first.

    02 · LinkSet next to the observed head.

    The candidate points to the current top node.

    03 · PublishCAS head from old to new.

    Only one contender can publish against that observed value.

    04 · RetryRe-use the refreshed expected value.

    If the CAS fails, update next and try again.

    Stack · push publication core
    Listing 7.2 idea · pp. 185–186
    #include <atomic>

template<typename T>
class push_only_stack_fragment
{
    struct node
    {
        T data;
        node* next;
        explicit node(T const& value)
            : data(value), next(nullptr) {}
    };

    std::atomic<node*> head;

public:
    push_only_stack_fragment() : head(nullptr) {}

    void push(T const& value)
    {
        node* const fresh = new node(value);
        fresh->next = head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        while (!head.compare_exchange_weak(
            fresh->next, fresh,
            std::memory_order_release,
            std::memory_order_relaxed))
        {}
    }
};
    Publish only after initialization: the successful release CAS makes the completed node visible to a matching acquire operation. A failed CAS only refreshes the expected pointer, so this example uses relaxed ordering on failure. This is deliberately a push-only fragment, not a complete stack.
    The hard part is pop()

    A successful CAS chooses one winner; it does not keep a node alive.

    Two poppers may read the same head. Compare/exchange prevents both from removing the same top node, but a losing thread may still be about to read old_head->next while the winner tries to reclaim that node.

    Returning a value also needs an exception-safe handoff. The chapter stores payload in a smart pointer so it can be moved out without allocating after the node has been removed.

    ProtectMake the node safe to read.
    ClaimCAS removes one head.
    RetireReclaim only when unreferenced.
    i Do not paste this fragment in as a finished container. It intentionally omits pop(), destruction, and safe reclamation. A simple CAS loop that dereferences a raw node pointer and then deletes it can have a use-after-free—even though the pointer itself is atomic.
    7.2.2–4
    The lifetime problem

    Retire a node first; free it only when no thread can still touch it.

    After removing a node from a shared list, another thread may hold a pointer it read earlier. Deleting immediately makes that pointer dangle. A correct lock-free structure therefore needs an explicit memory-reclamation strategy, not just an atomic head.

    Quiescent point

    Wait until no pop is active.

    Count active poppers and reclaim retired nodes when the count reaches zero. Easy to explain, but a steady stream of readers can postpone reclamation and let the retired list grow without bound.

    Hazard pointers

    Publish which node you may dereference.

    A reader publishes a hazard pointer, then rechecks the shared head before touching the node. Removed nodes are retired and freed only after a scan finds no hazard pointer to them. The publication protocol and its memory ordering must be correct.

    Reference counts

    Track outstanding access to each node.

    Split external and internal counts so a thread can safely acquire a reference before dereferencing a node. Delete only when the combined count reaches zero. Atomic shared_ptr operations are not guaranteed lock-free.

    Other options

    Garbage collection or deferred retirement.

    A collector can reclaim unreachable nodes automatically. Per-thread retire lists can batch scans and reduce shared contention, trading memory for lower reclamation overhead.

    Do not overlook node reuse

    Recycling trades allocator work for ABA risk.

    Reusing a node can prevent its address from becoming invalid, but it can also make an old pointer value appear current again. Reuse does not remove the need for a lifetime and ABA plan.

    7.2.5
    Audit before optimizing

    Derive the happens-before edges before weakening memory order.

    Start with the data that crosses threads and identify which write must become visible before which read. Only then choose the weakest ordering that establishes each required relationship.

    PrototypeBegin with memory_order_seq_cst.

    It gives sequentially consistent operations one total order and is easier to reason about while the algorithm is still changing.

    PublishRelease the fully initialized node.

    A release operation on publication can make earlier node initialization visible to a matching acquire that observes it.

    ObserveAcquire before reading ordinary node fields.

    In the counted-stack example, the successful acquire CAS that raises the external count provides the needed visibility before the node is dereferenced.

    RetryUse relaxed failure only when justified.

    A failed compare/exchange has not published the candidate; relaxed failure can be enough if the refreshed value is used only to retry. Reference-count cleanup has its own proof.

    ↔ Passing stress tests is not a memory-model proof. A rare visibility failure may not appear on the machine used for testing. Relax ordering only after reviewing all operations that can observe or mutate the structure; use a systematic checker where available.
    7.2.6
    A lock-free linked queue

    Separate head and tail—but let any thread finish an incomplete link.

    A single-producer, single-consumer queue can use atomic head and tail pointers with a dummy node. That alone is not safe for multiple producers or consumers: producers can race while filling the same tail, and consumers can race while removing the same head. The multi-threaded design needs CAS, counted pointers for lifetime, and helping.

    One dummy nodeThe tail always identifies the empty end.

    Each successful enqueue publishes data in the old dummy node, links a fresh dummy after it, then advances tail. Pop advances head to claim one item.

    Counted pointersProtect a snapshot before dereferencing it.

    External counters keep a node alive while a thread uses a head or tail snapshot; internal counts account for outstanding references after the external pointer moves.

    Help, don't spinFinish the visible next step for a stalled producer.

    If the tail data is already claimed, another producer can link a dummy node and advance tail rather than waiting for the original thread to resume.

    Interactive queue interleaving

      This is a teaching schedule, not a running concurrent program. Counted references keep the old node safe while A still holds it. A production queue also needs fully specified atomic orderings, exception handling, destruction rules, and a tested reclamation scheme.
