      7.3–4
      Design checklist

      Keep the proof, the memory scheme, and the progress story together.

      Lock-free code is difficult to get right and easy to test incompletely. These guidelines capture the recurring failure modes in the stack and queue examples.

      01
      Prototype with sequential consistency.

      Relax an operation only after identifying its required happens-before edges and proving the weaker order is sufficient.

      02
      Choose reclamation before writing pop().

      Track every path that may still hold a pointer. Never equate “unlinked” with “safe to delete.”

      03
      Review every compare/exchange for ABA.

      A value can change A → B → A while a thread is paused. A version tag combined atomically with the pointer can detect change; free-list reuse makes the risk more visible.

      04
      Turn waiting into helping—or choose a lock.

      A tight loop waiting for one owner to resume is effectively blocking and burns CPU. If another thread can complete the published next step, make that help part of the algorithm.

      05
      Check the whole implementation, not just the pointer.

      Verify atomic types are lock-free on the target; include reclamation, allocator behavior, contention, and the actual latency or throughput objective in measurements.

      06
      Prefer a proven component unless lock-free is needed.

      The complexity buys specific progress and resilience properties. A mutex-based structure is often simpler, safer, and faster for the workload.

      7.4 · Chapter summary

      Atomic updates are only one part of a correct concurrent structure.

      Lock-free stacks and queues rely on a proof that spans pointer publication, memory ordering, object lifetime, and progress. Helping can remove a busy wait, but it does not simplify the reclamation or platform questions.

      • Lock-free means system-wide progress; wait-free additionally bounds every thread's completion.
      • CAS prevents duplicate updates, but safe memory reclamation prevents use-after-free.
      • Release/acquire can publish node initialization; weaken other orders only after a full proof.
      • Use hazard pointers, reference counting, or another well-defined reclamation scheme; audit ABA and node reuse.
      • Help a stalled operation when possible, and benchmark against a clear lock-based baseline.

      Chapter 7 quick recall

      Try to answer before opening each note.

      Why is a spinlock nonblocking but not lock-free?

      It does not suspend in a blocking library call, but a thread paused while holding the flag can prevent every other thread from entering. Lock-free progress does not depend on one particular participant resuming.

      What extra guarantee does wait-free add?

      Lock-free algorithms guarantee that the system as a whole makes progress; wait-free algorithms guarantee that every individual operation completes within a bounded number of its own steps.

      Why can’t a successful pop CAS justify deleting the node immediately?

      Another thread may already hold a pointer it read before the CAS and may still be about to dereference it. Reclamation must wait until no such access remains.

      What is the central hazard-pointer protocol?

      A thread publishes the node it intends to access and rechecks the shared pointer before dereferencing it. Removed nodes are retired until a scan confirms that no hazard pointer protects them.

      How does release/acquire help publish a node?

      The publisher initializes the node before a release operation makes it reachable; an acquire operation that observes that publication establishes the visibility needed before reading ordinary node fields.

      How can a queue stay lock-free if a producer pauses mid-push?

      A competing producer can help link the next dummy node and advance the tail instead of spinning until the first producer returns. The helper then retries its own push from the new tail.

      What is the ABA problem, and what can detect it?

      A thread reads A, pauses while the value changes to B and back to A, then succeeds with a stale comparison. A version counter combined atomically with the value can reveal the intervening change.

      CHAPTER
      08
      Designing concurrent code · printed pp. 224–272

      The fastest design starts with the shape of the work—not the number of threads.

      Choose how work is divided, then design around what threads share, where data lives, and how failures and waits are handled. Parallel code is useful only when the whole design—not just its hot loop—benefits.

      8.1Divide the work 8.2Performance limits 8.3Data layout 8.4Scaling & safety 8.5Parallel algorithms 8.6Takeaways & recall
      8.1
      Choose a decomposition that fits the work

      Split by data, by emerging subproblems, or by responsibility.

      Ask what can run independently, when the boundaries are known, and how results will be combined. A good split creates enough parallel work without making coordination the new bottleneck.

      Known range · independent items

      Partition first; reduce afterward.

      For a fixed range, give workers contiguous blocks and let them process independently. Each can produce a local result; a final reduction combines those results. Count that combine step too—it may be parallelizable, or it may become the serial tail.

      Static blocks are simple when item costs are similar. Uneven work can leave one slow block holding up completion; smaller tasks can improve balance, but add scheduling and handoff overhead.

      Data-dependent · recursive

      Spawn subproblems only when they exist.

      In quicksort, the pivot reveals the independent partitions, so the work cannot be divided accurately up front. Recursively expose tasks, but stop splitting below a useful grain size and bound the number of active workers.

      A fixed worker pool can take pending chunks; a worker waiting for a result may help with other work. Creating a new operating-system thread at every recursive call risks oversubscription and runaway overhead.

      Streaming · task roles

      Use specialists when responsibilities differ.

      When input arrives over time, each thread can own one stage in a pipeline instead of every thread repeating the same operation on a different block. This also suits long-running background work alongside a responsive event loop.

      Keep the handoffs deliberate. If stages constantly share mutable state or wait on one another, the split may be wrong—or two responsibilities may belong together.

      A pipeline overlaps different items at different stages.Original teaching diagram · Chapter 8
      1. Stage 01ReadInput stream
      2. Stage 02DecodeParsed records
      3. Stage 03TransformIndependent work
      4. Stage 04WriteCompleted output

      Queues connect the stages. The slowest stage limits steady-state throughput; bounded queues and explicit cancellation help keep backlogs and shutdown behavior under control.

      8.2
      Performance is a hardware-and-workload property

      More runnable threads can make a program slower.

      Processors spend time moving cache lines, contending over shared state, and switching among ready tasks. A thread count that helps one workload or machine may hurt another.

      01

      Processor budget

      std::thread::hardware_concurrency() is only a hint and may return zero. It does not account for every other task in the process or on the machine. Bound CPU-bound work, and treat the value as a starting point rather than a guaranteed optimum.

      02

      Contention and cache ping-pong

      When cores repeatedly modify one counter, lock, or other hot location, ownership of its cache line moves between them. A relaxed atomic still needs exclusive access for a read-modify-write. Prefer per-worker partial state and combine or publish in batches when the algorithm allows it.

      03

      False sharing

      Distinct variables can occupy the same cache line. If different cores update those variables, cache coherence moves the line even though the program has no logical data sharing. Group data by the thread that owns it; add padding or alignment only when measurements show it helps.

      04

      Data proximity

      A thread that walks nearby elements can reuse cache lines. Scattered data and pointer chasing expand the working set and increase misses; context switches or migration can add more cache reloads. Keep a worker's common accesses spatially close where practical.

      05

      Oversubscription and switching

      Extra threads are useful when existing workers block on I/O. Too many ready-to-run, CPU-bound threads force time slicing, increase scheduling cost, and disrupt locality. Measure the workload and cap parallelism rather than spawning without a limit.

      ↗Measure the whole workload. Compare against a sequential baseline, vary the worker count and chunk size, and test on representative hardware. A pool can control thread creation, but its shared work queue can itself become a contended hot spot.
      8.3
      Correctness and speed are separate design questions

      Assign data so workers can do useful work with fewer cache misses.

      A structure can be perfectly race-free and still scale poorly. Data ownership, memory layout, and access patterns determine whether cores work independently or spend their time competing for cache lines.

      PartitionPotential benefitWhat to watch
      Adjacent rowsEach worker writes a contiguous region of a row-major result, which can improve output locality and reduce overlap on cache lines.A worker may still touch broad portions of the input matrices; compare input reuse and memory traffic.
      Adjacent columnsWorkers can own neighboring output columns and read related values from each row.Writes are strided across rows, and ownership boundaries can share cache lines. Measure the actual layout and access pattern.
      Rectangular tilesEach worker owns a compact output block and can reuse smaller regions of both inputs, reducing repeated data movement.Tile size, boundary alignment, and scheduling overhead matter; no partition wins for every matrix or machine.
      Matrix example · output ownership

      Give each worker a compact tile to write.

      This simplified 4×4 map assigns a separate 2×2 output tile to each worker. For matrix multiplication, a tile can reuse nearby input rows and columns while keeping output writes local. The same principle—minimize each worker's working set and avoid neighboring writers—applies to other large data structures too.

      AABB AABB CCDD CCDD

      Each letter represents one worker-owned block.

      Reduce hot writesAccumulate locally, then combine, instead of incrementing one global counter for every item.
      Keep nearby work togetherContiguous ranges often improve cache reuse; pointer-heavy trees may be harder to partition evenly.
      Use padding as a diagnosisTemporary padding can reveal false sharing; prefer measured ownership/layout changes over a guessed cache-line size.
      8.4
      Exceptions, speedup, waiting, and responsiveness

      Design the failure path and the serial ceiling before tuning.

      Parallel algorithms add failure paths across threads. Even a correct decomposition cannot scale past its serial work, and extra workers help only when they have something useful to do.

      Exception safety

      Worker exceptions need a route back.

      An exception escaping a std::thread entry function calls std::terminate; it does not propagate to the caller. Capture results and exceptions with a std::future from std::packaged_task, or another explicit channel. Use RAII to join every launched thread even if setup or foreground work throws, then observe worker failures before returning.

      Scalability · Amdahl's law

      Serial work limits ideal speedup.

      For a fixed workload, let s be the serial fraction and P the worker count. The ideal upper bound is:

      S(P) = 1 / (s + (1 − s) / P)
      Hide latency carefully

      Use idle time only when it is real.

      A worker blocked on I/O or a future leaves room for useful work. Additional workers—or helping while waiting—can hide that latency. The benefit depends on how long tasks wait; too many runnable CPU-heavy workers create oversubscription instead.

      Responsiveness · separate concerns

      Keep the event loop free to respond.

      Run long work away from a UI or event-processing thread. Send completion and progress back through messages, define cooperative cancellation, and join or otherwise manage the worker during shutdown. Keep UI updates on the UI thread.

      Amdahl's law · explore the serial ceiling

      Interactive study aid

      Adjust the fixed workload's serial share and the number of workers. This idealized model excludes task creation, synchronization, contention, I/O, and imbalance, so treat the result as a ceiling—not a benchmark prediction.

      SerialParallel
      Ideal speedup4.71×versus one worker
      Unlimited-worker ceiling10×set by the serial portion
      Worker efficiency58.8%ideal speedup ÷ workers

      With 10% serial work and 8 workers, the ideal fixed-work speedup is about 4.71×.

      If the serial share is zero, the formula has no finite ceiling; real programs still pay overhead. Reducing serial work and waiting matters more than adding workers past the point where useful parallel work runs out.

      8.5
      Three algorithms, three different constraints

      Parallelize the operation's semantics—not just its loop.

      The book's for_each, find, and partial_sum examples show why independent items, early completion, and prefix dependencies need different strategies.

      Independent map · std::for_each

      Split a range, preserve the contract.

      Contiguous chunks work well when each element can be processed independently. Calls may execute concurrently and in a different order than the sequential algorithm, so the function and any captured state must be safe under that contract. Join workers and propagate exceptions deliberately; use coarse blocks instead of creating one tiny task per element.

      Early result · std::find

      Stop searching when the answer is known.

      Searching every assigned block can erase the sequential algorithm's early-exit advantage. Workers can publish a match and observe a shared stop flag, but result publication must be synchronized and frequent atomic polling has a cost. Choose a sensible polling granularity and handle the no-match case too.

      Prefix dependency · std::partial_sum

      Local prefixes need the earlier carry.

      Each later chunk depends on totals from all earlier chunks. First compute local prefixes; then add the preceding chunks' totals to each block. A parallel tree scan can expose more concurrency, at the cost of extra work and synchronization. Preserve the operation's ordering requirements; floating-point addition may round differently when regrouped.

      Chunked prefix sum · numbers 1 through 6

      Split into two blocks[1, 2, 3]   |   [4, 5, 6]
      Compute local prefixes[1, 3, 6]   |   [4, 9, 15]
      Add the first block's total (6) to block two[1, 3, 6]   |   [10, 15, 21]
      01Choose a grain size that amortizes scheduling without leaving a long straggler.
      02Account for reduction, cancellation, output ordering, and all other dependencies.
      03Define how exceptions and partial results reach the caller; always clean up workers.
      04Benchmark the complete operation against a sequential baseline on target hardware.
      8.6 · Chapter summary

      Scale by reducing waiting and data movement—not by multiplying threads.

      Start from the algorithm's dependencies, give each worker a clear slice of work and data, and measure how the whole design behaves. Performance optimizations never replace exception safety or a correct synchronization plan.

      • Choose static ranges, recursive tasks, or a pipeline to match when work becomes available.
      • Limit hot shared writes, false sharing, scattered access, and oversubscription.
      • Keep data ownership and cache locality in mind when laying out structures and partitions.
      • Use Amdahl's law to expose the serial ceiling; hide latency only when extra work can use the idle time.
      • Propagate worker exceptions, join reliably, and benchmark the sequential and parallel versions.

      Chapter 8 quick recall

      Try to answer before opening each note.

      When should work be split up front, and when recursively?

      Split a known range up front when elements are independent and their work is reasonably uniform. Use recursive or queued tasks when processing reveals new independent subproblems; bound workers and stop at a useful grain size.

      What does a pipeline trade for its overlap?

      Specialist stages can process different items at once, but queues, imbalance, and communication couple the stages. The slowest stage limits steady-state throughput.

      Why can a relaxed atomic counter still scale poorly?

      Relaxed ordering removes ordering constraints on other memory, but a read-modify-write still needs exclusive ownership of the counter's cache line. Contending cores can bounce that line repeatedly.

      What is false sharing?

      Different threads update distinct variables that happen to occupy the same cache line. Coherence traffic occurs even though the program has no logical sharing between those variables.

      What does Amdahl's law predict?

      For serial fraction s and P workers, ideal speedup is at most 1 / (s + (1 − s) / P). Even infinitely many workers cannot remove the serial portion.

      How should an exception from a worker reach its caller?

      Capture it in a future or another explicit error channel, join all started threads using RAII, and retrieve/rethrow the error on a thread that can handle it. An uncaught exception at a raw thread entry point terminates the program.

      Why is parallel find more than splitting the range?

      It can finish before every element is inspected. Workers need a safe way to publish a match and stop unnecessary work, while polling and synchronization must not cost more than the saved search.

      Why can't partial_sum be reduced to independent chunks alone?

      Every chunk's first result depends on the total of all preceding chunks. Compute local prefixes, then propagate earlier totals—or use a parallel scan when its extra work and operation-order requirements are acceptable.

      ↗Source: Anthony Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action: Practical Multithreading, Chapter 8, printed pp. 224–272. The pipeline, tile map, and Amdahl calculator are original study aids.
      CHAPTER
      09
      Advanced thread management · printed pp. 273–299

      Reuse bounded workers, make task dependencies explicit, and stop work cooperatively.

      A thread pool separates task submission from worker lifetime. Its scheduler must avoid starvation and queue contention; its shutdown path must preserve task and object lifetimes. Cancellation is a request for a thread to stop safely—not permission to terminate it mid-operation.

      9.1Thread pools 9.1.2–3Results & dependencies 9.1.4–5Queues & stealing 9.2Cooperative stop 9.2.3–7Waits & shutdown 9.3Summary & recall
      9.1
      Keep workers; submit tasks

      A pool reuses a bounded set of threads for many small jobs.

      Callers enqueue work instead of creating a new operating-system thread for every task. Workers repeatedly take pending tasks, execute them, and return for more.

      Bound the workers

      Keep thread lifetime separate from task lifetime.

      A fixed worker set avoids per-task thread startup and limits concurrent execution. Hardware concurrency can be a starting hint, not an exact answer; handle a zero hint and consider the workload and other work on the system.

      Return a task handle

      Use futures for results and failures.

      A waitable submit() can wrap a callable in std::packaged_task and return its std::future. The future carries the result or captured exception back to the caller. Task submission and waiting both have overhead, so choose a useful task size.

      Plan shutdown

      Stop workers before destroying their queue.

      Define whether shutdown drains queued tasks or abandons them, stop accepting work at the right time, wake idle workers, and join them before shared pool state is destroyed. A pool's destructor policy is part of its contract.

      Callersubmit(task)keeps a future
      →
      Pending workShared queuewaits for a worker
      →
      Worker ARun taskthen fetch more
      Worker BRun anothersame fixed pool
      ↗C++11 implementation detail. std::packaged_task is move-only, while std::function requires a copyable target. The book uses a small move-only type-erasure wrapper for queued tasks. A production pool also needs a clear exception, admission, and shutdown policy.
      9.1.2–3
      A future can wait—and waiting can consume capacity

      Nested task dependencies can deadlock a small pool.

      Independent tasks fit a basic pool. But if every worker runs a parent task, submits a child, and blocks on that child's future, the queued children have no free worker to execute them.

      01

      Parent tasks occupy the pool.

      Worker A runs Parent A; Worker B runs Parent B. Each parent submits a child task and then calls future.get().

      02

      All workers block; children stay queued.

      If both workers wait, the queue still contains Child A and Child B, but no worker can pick either one up. More queued work cannot help when every worker is blocked.

      03

      Let a waiter help the pool.

      While waiting for its result, a worker can run pending work—such as run_pending_task()—until the future becomes ready. A dependency-aware scheduler can provide the same kind of progress.

      Pool dependency lab · can either child task run?

      Two workers each run a parent task that submits one child. Step through the schedule to see why blocking all workers can strand queued work—and how helping frees the dependency chain.

      Worker state2 workers
      Worker AAvailable
      Worker BAvailable
      Pending queue0 tasks

        Press “Next event” to submit the parent tasks.

          0 / 2
          9.1.4–5
          Reduce queue contention without losing balance

          Local queues improve locality; work stealing redistributes idle time.

          A single shared queue is simple but makes every submission and task pickup contend on the same structure. Per-thread queues reduce that traffic, but a busy thread can still hold all the work.

          One global queue

          Easy to schedule, easy to contend on.

          All producers enqueue and all workers dequeue from one shared place. As worker count rises, that hot queue can bounce between caches and limit throughput—even if the queue is lock-free.

          Thread-local queues

          Keep a worker near its own tasks.

          A pool thread can put newly spawned work on its local queue, while external submissions enter a shared queue. This reduces common-case synchronization, but uneven task trees can leave one queue full and others empty.

          Work stealing

          Let idle workers borrow from a busy peer.

          Try local work first, then global work, then steal from another worker. Stealing balances irregular recursive workloads; each queue still needs safe synchronization and stealing itself has a cost.

          Queue ownerPop newest · LIFO
          Newest taskNext taskOlder task
          Owner endSteal end
          Idle peerSteal oldest · FIFO
          ↔Why opposite ends? The owner can keep taking its newest task, often close to the data it just touched; a thief takes older work from the far end. This is a common work-stealing pattern, not a universal queue policy.
          9.2
          Cancellation without unsafe forced termination

          Stopping a thread is cooperative: signal it, wake it, let it clean up.

          A thread can stop only when its code reaches a safe cancellation point or a blocking operation that knows how to respond. If it never checks the request—or sleeps forever in an unrelated wait—it may never finish.

          01 · Request

          Publish a stop signal.

          The controller sets a flag or requests stop through a token. The signal says “please finish”; it does not asynchronously kill the worker or roll back a half-written invariant.

          02 · Observe

          Check at safe points.

          Check between bounded units of work, or use an interruptible wait. Put checks where the operation can unwind without leaving shared state inconsistent.

          03 · Finish

          Unwind, release, and join.

          Use RAII for locks and resources, publish any final status, and join the thread. A cancellation exception must be handled inside the thread wrapper; escaping a raw std::thread entry function calls std::terminate.

          Modern C++ note: C++20 adds std::jthread and std::stop_token.

          The book's custom C++11 design checks a thread-local flag at explicit interruption points and throws a dedicated thread_interrupted exception; its thread wrapper catches that signal at the boundary. C++11 itself has no standard stop token. A C++20 stop request is still cooperative: the function must check its token, and a regular blocking wait is not magically interrupted. std::jthread requests stop and joins on destruction; it cannot make an unresponsive worker safe by force.

          C++20 · bounded work and cooperative stop
          Modern standard-library note
          #include <chrono>
#include <stop_token>
#include <thread>

void background(std::stop_token stop)
{
    while (!stop.stop_requested())
    {
        // Replace with one bounded unit of work.
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(20));
    }
}

int main()
{
    std::jthread worker(background);
    worker.request_stop();
    // Destruction also requests stop, then joins.
}
          The short wait is only a demonstration: a production worker should use a cancellation-aware wait where possible, or a bounded timeout. Stop requests never guarantee instant interruption.
          9.2.3–7
          Interruptible waits and orderly application exit

          Wake blocked workers deliberately—and request every stop before joining.

          Setting a flag cannot wake a thread that is asleep on a condition variable, future, or I/O operation. The wait and cancellation signal must share a safe wake-up protocol.

          Condition-variable waits

          A naive “set flag, notify, then wait” can lose a notification if the request lands between the final check and the wait. Register the wake-up safely with the wait protocol, use a stop-aware wait where available, or use a timed wait as a bounded polling fallback. Recheck the predicate after waking.

          Other blocking calls

          For a future, mutex, or I/O operation without a cancellation facility, use its own wake-up mechanism or a timeout loop and check the request between waits. Shorter polling intervals improve response time but cause more wakeups and scheduling overhead.

          C++20 condition-variable detail.

          std::condition_variable_any has stop-token-aware wait overloads. With C++11's std::condition_variable, design the notification and predicate protocol so a stop signal cannot be missed; merely adding an atomic flag beside wait() is not sufficient.

          First · signal allRequest stop from every background worker.

          Let independent workers begin cleanup concurrently.

          Then · cooperateReach a checkpoint and release resources.

          Wake stop-aware waits and preserve invariants.

          Finally · joinWait for all workers before destroying state.

          Do not free queues or shared objects while a worker can still use them.

          ✓Why request all stops first? If the controller interrupts one worker and immediately joins it, it may sit idle while other workers keep running. Signal all workers, then join; their cleanup can proceed in parallel.
          9.3 · Chapter summary

          Thread management is about keeping work schedulable and lifetimes ordered.

          A pool amortizes worker creation, but its queue and dependency policy determine whether tasks can make progress. Cooperative cancellation works only when waiting, cleanup, and shutdown all participate in the protocol.

          • Submit tasks to a bounded worker set; return futures when callers need results or exceptions.
          • Choose task granularity large enough to justify queueing, scheduling, and future overhead.
          • Prevent pool starvation when tasks wait for subtasks; let workers help or use a dependency-aware scheduler.
          • Use local queues to reduce contention and work stealing to rebalance uneven task trees.
          • Cancellation is cooperative: define safe points, wake blocking waits, clean up, and join before destroying shared state.

          Chapter 9 quick recall

          Try to answer before opening each note.

          What does a thread pool reuse?

          A bounded set of worker threads. Tasks are queued and executed by available workers, so callers do not create and join a new thread for every task.

          How can a pool return a task's value or exception?

          Wrap the callable in a packaged task, retain its future, and let the caller get the result. Exceptions captured by the task are rethrown by get().

          How can nested task waits deadlock a fixed-size pool?

          If every worker blocks waiting for child work that is still queued, no worker is available to run that work. A waiter can run pending tasks or the scheduler can understand dependencies.

          How do local queues and work stealing complement each other?

          Local queues reduce contention and improve locality for the owner. An idle worker steals from another queue to rebalance work; the owner often takes recent work while thieves take from the opposite end.

          Does a stop request forcibly interrupt a thread?

          No. The worker must observe the request at a cancellation point or through a wait designed to wake. It then needs to release resources safely and finish.

          Why is setting a flag not enough to interrupt a condition-variable wait?

          A blocked thread cannot check the flag, and a notification can be lost if it arrives just before the thread actually waits. Couple the stop signal to the wait protocol or use an appropriate stop-aware/timed wait.

          Why signal all background threads before joining any?

          That allows all of them to begin cleanup together while the controller still has useful work to do. Joining after all stop requests can reduce shutdown time.

          ↗Source: Anthony Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action: Practical Multithreading, Chapter 9, printed pp. 273–299. The pool dependency lab is an original study aid; the std::jthread note reflects C++20 and is not part of the 2012 text.
          CHAPTER
          10
          Testing and debugging multithreaded applications · printed pp. 300–314

          A passing test is evidence about the schedules you exercised—not proof that every interleaving is safe.

          Concurrency bugs can depend on rare timing, hide behind innocent-looking operations, and show symptoms far from the fault. Make the concurrent surface small, review assumptions explicitly, control the schedules you can, then stress and measure on representative hardware.

          10.1Bug patterns 10.2.1Review checklist 10.2.2Testing strategies 10.2.3Design for tests 10.2.4–5Control the start 10.2.6Measure scaling 10.3Summary & recall
          10.1
          Name the failure before choosing a test

          Concurrency bugs cluster around unwanted waiting and harmful races.

          The same symptom—a hang, crash, or wrong answer—can have a different cause. Classify the failure and identify the invariant or progress guarantee that was violated.

          Unwanted blocking

          Waiting can stop useful progress.

          Deadlock: threads wait on a cycle and none can proceed. Livelock: threads keep reacting or retrying, often burning CPU, but useful work does not advance. A worker blocked indefinitely on external input can also strand tasks that depend on it.

          Broken shared-state invariants

          A race can corrupt an otherwise valid structure.

          Two individually valid operations may interleave in an invalid order. Symptoms include duplicate removal, stale results, partially updated state, dangling pointers, double-free, or lost work. The broken invariant can be temporal—an operation happened too early—as well as about a value.

          Lifetime and visibility

          Data can disappear before its last reader.

          A thread may outlive a local object it references, an exception may skip a needed join(), or an unsynchronized access may expose an invalid view of shared state. These faults often surface later and elsewhere as apparently random memory corruption.

          Scheduling race · may be benign

          Which worker dequeues the next independent job?

          The outcome depends on scheduling, but if every worker may safely take that job, the variation is part of the design rather than a bug.

          C++ data race · undefined behavior

          Conflicting non-atomic accesses without synchronization.

          This is a narrower, language-defined problem—not a synonym for every scheduling race. Protect shared state with a valid mutex/atomic protocol; otherwise the program has undefined behavior.

          10.2.1
          Code review · read what the threads can do, not what you intended

          Walk the shared data, lock ownership, ordering, and lifetimes.

          Read the code as if another thread were running at every point where the current one pauses, unlocks, calls out, or returns. Explain each transition in terms of the invariant it preserves.

          01

          What is shared—and who protects it?

          List mutable state, every read/write path, and the exact mutex or atomic protocol. Look for references or pointers that let callers bypass that protection.

          02

          Which locks are held, and in what order?

          Check every call made while locked, every nested lock, callbacks, and lock reacquisition. After releasing a mutex, assume another thread may have changed the data.

          03

          What may another thread do right now?

          Challenge each “this can’t happen” assumption. Check whether a check-then-act sequence is one atomic operation or whether another thread can slip between the calls.

          04

          Can every exit path clean up safely?

          Trace exceptions, cancellation, early returns, object destruction, and thread joins. Prove that no worker can access an object after its lifetime ends.

          10.2.2–4
          Small tests, stress runs, and schedule exploration

          Test the smallest useful concurrent unit—and vary the conditions.

          Run ordinary single-threaded tests for the nonconcurrent logic, then target the shared component with scenarios designed to create the risky interactions. One green run cannot cover an unvisited schedule.

          Start narrow

          Test the concurrent component directly.

          Exercise a queue, state machine, or synchronization boundary without a large application around it. Separate ordinary functional failures from concurrency-specific failures, and assert the final invariant—not merely that the test did not crash.

          Stress · build confidence

          Repeat runs, but do not mistake repetition for proof.

          More runs, workers, and inputs make rare schedules more likely to appear. A stress test can still miss them if the test harness or hardware never permits the problematic interleaving.

          Explore · control execution

          Use tools that expose other schedules.

          Model/combination simulation can explore permitted interleavings for small tests, but the search grows rapidly. Instrumented synchronization libraries can check lock discipline, report inconsistent lock orders, or let a test control which waiter proceeds.

          Boundary statesEmpty, partially full, and full queues; zero items and more consumers than items.
          Operation mixesOne producer/consumer, many producers, many consumers, and mixed push/pop traffic.
          EnvironmentOne and many workers, different core counts, and representative processor architectures.
          Modern tool note · dynamic race detectors complement tests.

          Tools such as ThreadSanitizer can report data races observed during an executed test. A clean run does not prove all schedules safe, and race detection alone does not establish liveness, correct results, or absence of deadlock.

          10.2.3
          Design for testability before the bug arrives

          Keep the synchronization boundary small and the logic easy to exercise.

          Short, single-responsibility operations and control over the test environment make it easier to isolate the behavior that truly needs concurrent execution.

          Separate

          Test pure work without threads.

          Split reading shared state, transforming it, and writing results. Test transformations and per-thread state machines with ordinary single-threaded tests; reserve concurrent tests for communication and shared-state invariants.

          Control

          Make dependencies replaceable.

          Inject clocks, queues, schedulers, and event sources where practical. Small test doubles can generate the exact inputs or notifications the real environment would produce.

          Audit

          Do not overlook library state.

          A library call may hide internal mutable state. Check whether it is safe for concurrent use, protect it, or select an alternative with the required thread-safety guarantee.

          10.2.4–5
          Arrange the test's “while” moment

          Start workers together, then assert the complete outcome.

          Separate a test into shared setup, per-thread setup, the concurrent operations, and postconditions. Readiness promises and a shared start gate can keep workers poised until the harness releases them.

          Schedule lab · does this test actually create overlap?

          Assume a blocking queue starts empty. One worker calls push(42); another calls pop(). The uncoordinated path shows one possible serialized schedule, not a guarantee; independently launched threads may overlap by chance. The model is not a real scheduler: a shared gate makes both workers ready to run, but does not force a particular instruction-by-instruction interleaving.

          Producer threadNot startedReady signal: no
          Consumer threadNot startedReady signal: no
          Shared start gateNot releasedWorkers ready: 0 / 2
          PostconditionNot checkedpop returns 42 · queue empty

          Press “Next step” to begin the selected test schedule.

            0 / 2
            C++11 · readiness gate pattern
            Queue supplies push(), blocking pop(), and empty()
            #include <future>
#include <stdexcept>

template<typename Queue>
void test_push_pop_overlap(Queue& q)
{
    std::promise<void> go, push_ready, pop_ready;
    std::shared_future<void> start(go.get_future());
    std::future<void> pushed;
    std::future<int> popped;
    std::future<void> producer_ready = push_ready.get_future();
    std::future<void> consumer_ready = pop_ready.get_future();

    try
    {
        pushed = std::async(std::launch::async, [&q, start, &push_ready] {
            push_ready.set_value();
            start.wait();
            q.push(42);
        });
        popped = std::async(std::launch::async, [&q, start, &pop_ready] {
            pop_ready.set_value();
            start.wait();
            return q.pop();
        });
        producer_ready.wait();
        consumer_ready.wait();
        go.set_value();

        pushed.get();
        if (popped.get() != 42 || !q.empty())
            throw std::runtime_error("push/pop postcondition failed");
    }
    catch (...)
    {
        try { go.set_value(); }
        catch (std::future_error const&) { }
        throw;
    }
}
            Declare the async futures outside the try so cleanup can release the gate before their destructors wait. This compact sketch assumes worker operations complete normally; a production harness must define cleanup for worker exceptions. Futures from std::async do not cancel a stuck task on destruction, so enforce deadlock timeouts at the test-process boundary.
            10.2.6
            Performance testing · verify the reason you added concurrency

            Measure the scaling curve, not just one fast run.

            Concurrency can improve throughput or latency on one system and regress on another. Serial work, contention, scheduling overhead, and memory behavior all change as the core count grows.

            Choose a baseline

            Compare with the sequential design.

            Measure the same useful work with one worker and with the parallel implementation. State whether the goal is lower latency for one task or more throughput across many tasks.

            Vary the machine

            Test small and large core counts.

            Check at least a low-concurrency and a high-concurrency system when available. Contention can look harmless with two workers and dominate with many; a single-core run is not a substitute for multicore testing.

            Explain regressions

            Relate the curve to the design.

            Use the serial fraction to estimate an upper bound, then investigate queue/lock contention, task grain size, cache traffic, and oversubscription when measurements fall short or flatten.

            ↗Interpret results honestly. A stress test that passed is not proof against a schedule it never reached; a fast benchmark on one processor count is not proof of scalability. Record the tested inputs, worker counts, platform, and limitations.
            10.3 · Chapter summary

            Test the contract, control the setup, and be explicit about what remains untested.

            Concurrency testing is difficult because schedules vary and failures can surface far from their cause. Small focused tests, careful reviews, controlled start conditions, stress runs, and representative performance measurements build complementary evidence.

            • Distinguish benign scheduling variation from harmful races and C++ data races.
            • Review shared state, lock ownership/order, operation boundaries, exception paths, and lifetimes.
            • Exercise boundary cases and mixed operations; coordinate readiness before testing overlap.
            • Stress tests and dynamic tools help, but neither proves every schedule safe.
            • Measure against a sequential baseline across representative worker counts and hardware.

            Chapter 10 quick recall

            Try to answer before opening each note.

            How does a race condition differ from a C++ data race?

            A race condition is any scheduling-dependent behavior and may be benign. A data race is the narrower case of conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory location, with at least one non-atomic access; in C++ it causes undefined behavior.

            What is the difference between deadlock and livelock?

            Deadlocked threads are blocked waiting in a cycle. Livelocked threads keep executing or retrying, often using CPU, but fail to make useful progress.

            Why can repeated stress tests give false confidence?

            They sample only schedules the test harness and hardware actually produce. A rare interleaving—or one impossible on the test machine—may never occur, no matter how many times the same test is repeated.

            What does a readiness gate guarantee?

            It confirms each worker has reached a known point before the controller releases them. It creates an opportunity for overlap; it does not force the exact order of operations after release.

            Why test the same code on different processor counts?

            Contention and scheduling costs change with the number of cores. Code that scales on a small machine may flatten or regress as more processors compete for shared state.

            ↗Source: Anthony Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action: Practical Multithreading, Chapter 10, printed pp. 300–314. The schedule lab and its explanatory diagram are original study aids; the race-detector note reflects modern tooling.
            APPENDIX
            A
            Brief reference for some C++11 language features · printed pp. 315–339

            The language features behind modern C++ concurrency APIs.

            This is the book’s next section after Chapter 10—not a numbered Chapter 11. Most of these features are general C++, but move semantics, forwarding, lambdas, and thread_local make thread-library code practical to write and read.

            A.1References & moves A.2–3Delete & default A.4constexpr A.5Lambdas & captures A.6Parameter packs A.7auto A.8thread_local A.9Summary & recall
            Reading note · this appendix describes C++11 as it stood in 2012.

            Some rules—especially the restrictions on constexpr functions—were relaxed by later C++ standards. The examples below are labeled C++11 where relevant; use a current language reference for today’s exact rules.

            A.1
            Rvalue references · move semantics · forwarding

            Move resources when copying would be wasteful—or meaningless.

            An lvalue names an object with an identity; an rvalue is typically a temporary. An rvalue-reference overload can accept a temporary and transfer its resources instead of duplicating them.

            Copy

            Build a second resource-owning object.

            A copy must preserve the original, so dynamic storage may need a separate allocation and duplicate contents.

            source owns data→copy owns duplicate
            Move

            Transfer ownership; keep the source valid.

            A move constructor can take a resource handle and leave the source in a valid moved-from state. Its exact post-move value is type-specific.

            source owns data⇢destination owns data
            Named rvalue references are lvalues

            Inside void f(T&& value), the expression value is named and therefore an lvalue. Use std::move(value) when you intentionally want to offer it to a move overload.

            std::move is a cast

            It does not move anything by itself. It enables overload resolution to select a move constructor or assignment operator; that operation performs the transfer.

            Forwarding references preserve intent

            When T is deduced, a parameter T&& can accept either category. std::forward<T> passes an lvalue on as an lvalue and an rvalue on as an rvalue.

            Ownership lab

            Move a unique_ptr without copying its object.

            Illustrates ownership, not scheduler behavior
            Source pointerOwns Widget
            ⇢
            Destination pointerEmpty

            Before the move, exactly one pointer owns the Widget.

            C++11 · a move-only owner
            The source unique_ptr becomes empty
            #include <memory>
#include <utility>

struct Widget {};

int main()
{
    std::unique_ptr<Widget> source(new Widget);
    std::unique_ptr<Widget> destination(std::move(source));
    // destination owns the Widget; source is now empty
}
            Unlike the general moved-from state, std::unique_ptr specifies that the source becomes empty after a successful move. Moving from a named object is an explicit signal that its old value may be relinquished.
            C++11 · forwarding a callable and its arguments
            A variadic wrapper like std::thread
            #include <thread>
#include <utility>

template<class Callable, class... Args>
void run_on_thread(Callable&& callable, Args&&... args)
{
    std::thread worker(
        std::forward<Callable>(callable),
        std::forward<Args>(args)...);
    worker.join();
}
            The deduced template types remember which arguments arrived as lvalues. The paired pack expansion forwards each argument with that original value category, so lvalues are not accidentally moved.
            A.2–3
            Deleted and defaulted special members

            Make ownership rules visible in the class interface.

            Use = delete to reject an operation at compile time, and = default to request the compiler-generated implementation while stating that choice explicitly.

            Delete what has no coherent meaning

            A mutex cannot be copied into a second owner.

            Deleting copy construction and copy assignment documents the contract and gives a compile-time diagnostic. A move-only type can delete copies and provide move operations for explicit ownership transfer.

            Default what should remain compiler-generated

            Preserve intent without hand-writing boilerplate.

            Default constructors, destructors, copy/move constructors, and copy/move assignments can be explicitly defaulted. A defaulted function is only trivial when the language’s other conditions are satisfied.

            Deleted overloads are useful beyond copying

            Reject an unwanted conversion deliberately.

            A deleted overload still participates in overload resolution. For example, an int overload marked deleted can prevent an implicit narrowing conversion to a short overload.

            C++11 · movable, deliberately noncopyable
            One owner at a time
            #include <memory>

class exclusive_owner
{
    std::unique_ptr<int> data;
public:
    exclusive_owner() : data(new int(42)) {}
    exclusive_owner(exclusive_owner const&) = delete;
    exclusive_owner& operator=(exclusive_owner const&) = delete;
    exclusive_owner(exclusive_owner&&) = default;
    exclusive_owner& operator=(exclusive_owner&&) = default;
};
            Move operations must be declared explicitly here because declaring copy operations suppresses implicit move generation. In a real class, the members’ own copy/move capabilities also determine which defaulted operations are available.
            A.4
            Constant expressions · literal types · static initialization

            constexpr can move initialization work to compile time.

            A constexpr function is eligible to produce a constant expression when called with suitable constant inputs; it can still be called at runtime with ordinary inputs. A constexpr object is const and must be initialized from a constant expression.

            Compile-time use

            In the book’s C++11 rules, a simple single-return function can supply an array bound or template argument when its inputs are constant expressions.

            Literal class types

            A suitable literal type and constexpr constructor can make a user-defined object constant-initialized, not just an integer.

            Concurrency connection

            Constant initialization is complete before dynamic initialization, avoiding some cross-translation-unit initialization-order hazards for global synchronization state.

            C++11 · a constant expression when the input is constant
            The same function may also run at runtime
            constexpr int square(int value)
{
    return value * value;
}

constexpr int extent = square(5);
int values[extent]; // 25 elements
            The expression square(5) is constant-evaluable; square(runtime_value) is an ordinary call if the argument is not constant. C++11 imposed much tighter body restrictions than later standards.
            A.5
            Callable objects at the point of use

            Capture by value for a snapshot; capture by reference for a live dependency.

            A lambda packages behavior with its captured state. In concurrent code, capture mode and lifetime matter: a worker must not retain a reference to a local object after that object has been destroyed.

            [value] · snapshot

            Own a copy of the value.

            The closure keeps the value from the moment it was created. This is usually the safer choice when returning or storing a callable, provided copying the captured object is appropriate.

            [&value] · reference

            Read or modify the original object.

            The closure observes the current value, but the referenced object must outlive every call. In a thread task, make sure the owning scope cannot exit too early.

            [this] · object access

            Capture the object pointer explicitly.

            Inside a member function, capture this to access members. It does not extend the object’s lifetime; the object must remain alive while the lambda runs.

            Capture lab

            What does the lambda see after the local changes?

            The lambda was created when offset was 10; the local is now 20. The lambda is called with 1 while the local is still alive.

            Captured value10
            Current local20
            Result of call(1)11

            By-value capture keeps the snapshot: 10 + 1 = 11.

            C++11 · two capture policies
            Both lambdas are called before offset leaves scope
            int main()
{
    int offset = 10;
    auto snapshot = [offset](int n) { return offset + n; };
    auto live = [&offset](int n) { return offset + n; };
    offset = 20;

    int snapshot_result = snapshot(1); // 11
    int live_result = live(1);         // 21
    return snapshot_result == 11 && live_result == 21 ? 0 : 1;
}
            A reference capture is not a snapshot, and it is not ownership. Returning or scheduling a lambda that refers to a short-lived local can create a dangling reference.
            A.6
            Variadic templates · parameter packs · pack expansion

            One template can accept and forward an arbitrary number of typed arguments.

            A parameter pack is expanded with ... into a type list or function-argument list. This is how APIs such as std::thread accept a callable followed by any number of arguments.

            Collect

            class... Args declares a template parameter pack; Args&&... args declares the matching function parameters.

            Expand

            std::forward<Args>(args)... repeats the expression once per argument, preserving each argument’s value category.

            Count

            sizeof...(Args) gives the pack length as a compile-time constant expression, including zero for an empty pack.

            C++11 · count a parameter pack
            A minimal variadic template
            template<class... Args>
unsigned count_args(Args const&...)
{
    return sizeof...(Args);
}

// count_args(42, 3.14, 'x') returns 3
            Pack expansions can also build tuples, declare function parameters, and expand forwarding expressions. The std::thread constructor uses this pattern to store and later invoke a callable with its arguments.
            A.7
            Automatic type deduction, still at compile time

            auto shortens a declaration; it does not make C++ dynamically typed.

            The compiler deduces the declared type from the initializer. Plain auto generally drops top-level references and cv-qualification; add & or const when that distinction matters.

            auto iterator = table.find(key);Deduce the iterator type from the expression.
            auto value = existing_ref;Plain auto deduces a value type, not a reference.
            auto& alias = existing_ref;The declarator explicitly preserves the lvalue reference.
            auto pointer = array;Array-to-pointer decay applies in this deduction context.
            A.8
            Per-thread storage duration

            thread_local creates one object per thread—not a shared object with a hidden lock.

            It can be used for namespace-scope variables, static data members, and local variables. A function-local thread-local object is initialized separately on the first passage through its declaration in each thread.

            Useful for

            State that truly belongs to one worker.

            Per-thread counters, caches, or scratch state can avoid contention when no other thread needs direct access.

            Lifetime still matters

            Do not publish a pointer past the owning thread’s lifetime.

            Each thread’s instance is destroyed as that thread exits. A pointer to it does not extend its lifetime, and cross-thread access still needs a safe protocol.

            C++11 · each thread has its own counter
            Per-thread state is not shared state
            thread_local unsigned work_count = 0;

void record_completed_task()
{
    ++work_count; // this thread's instance
}
            Thread-local storage does not make a pointer to the object safe to share. Also account for initialization and destruction order when one thread-local object depends on another.
            A.9 · Appendix summary

            These features clarify ownership, lifetime, and generic interfaces.

            Move operations transfer resources; deleted/defaulted functions express class contracts; lambdas and packs make small callable tasks concise; auto keeps declarations readable; and thread_local gives genuinely per-thread state.

            • Use std::move only when the source may be treated as an rvalue; it is a cast, not the move itself.
            • Forward deduced parameters with std::forward; initialize and use moved-from objects according to their type’s contract.
            • Use = delete and = default to make special-member policy explicit.
            • Choose lambda captures with both value semantics and the callable’s lifetime in mind.
            • thread_local isolates per-thread state but does not replace a sharing or lifetime protocol.

            Appendix A quick recall

            Try to answer before opening each note.

            Does std::move(x) move x?

            No. It casts the expression so a move overload can be selected. The selected operation decides what resources, if any, are transferred.

            Why does std::forward<T> need the deduced type?

            The deduced type records whether the original argument was an lvalue or rvalue, allowing forwarding to preserve that category.

            When is a reference capture unsafe?

            When the referenced object can be destroyed before the lambda’s last call—for example, when a background task outlives the local scope.

            What does thread_local guarantee?

            Each thread has its own instance. It does not synchronize access to that instance if a pointer or reference is deliberately shared with another thread.

            ↗Source: Anthony Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action: Practical Multithreading, Appendix A, “Brief reference for some C++11 language features,” printed pp. 315–339. The move-ownership and lambda-capture labs are original study aids; C++11 examples are kept distinct from later-standard notes.

            Compare
            The same label can hide different contracts

            Portability is not semantic equivalence.

            Map the behavior you need—ownership, wake-up, cancellation, and lifetime—before translating an API by name.

            Locks and waits

            A monitor is not a condition variable.

            Java’s intrinsic monitor combines mutual exclusion and waiting conventions. In C++, a condition variable works with a mutex and a predicate that must be rechecked; the synchronization protocol is explicit.

            Volatile is not a shared-memory protocol

            Do not translate Java volatile into C++ volatile.

            The two languages assign different concurrency meaning to that keyword. In C++ use atomics or locks that express the required ordering; ordinary volatile does not make a data race safe.

            Cancellation varies widely

            Interruption is a contract, not a method name.

            Java and Boost expose interruption mechanisms; POSIX cancellation has its own rules. C++11 std::thread has no standardized interruption API, so cancellation must be designed cooperatively.

            Standard-library accuracy note · futures.

            This guide lists the standardized C++11 std::future and std::shared_future types. The 2012 source matrix also prints std::atomic_future, which is not a standardized C++11 library type; do not rely on it as portable C++11.

            Use
            How to read a cross-library comparison

            Choose the abstraction that makes the required guarantee clear.

            01

            Start with the contract.

            Ask whether you need a joinable thread, mutual exclusion, predicate wait, result/exception transport, or bounded task execution.

            02

            Check what the standard actually supplies.

            C++11 gives threads, locks, condition variables, atomics, and futures—but not a general thread pool, concurrent-container suite, or standardized thread-interruption method.

            03

            Keep portability and policy separate.

            A portable API can wrap platform threads, but shutdown policy, fairness, cancellation, and performance still depend on its contract and implementation.

            Appendix B · study summary

            Use the matrix to orient yourself, then verify the semantics.

            The comparison is a map of where common facilities live, not a promise that similarly named APIs behave identically or exist in every current release.

            • Threads, locks, waits, atomics, futures, pools, and interruption are provided at different layers in each ecosystem.
            • The C++11 standard library stops short of prescribing a thread pool or general concurrent-container collection.
            • Condition-variable predicates, memory ordering, cancellation, and object lifetimes still need a language-appropriate design.
            • Use chapter references to follow the C++ design details rather than porting API names mechanically.

            Appendix B quick recall

            Try to answer before opening each note.

            Does C++11 provide a standard thread pool or thread interruption method?

            No. The standard supplies std::thread and synchronization primitives, but applications or libraries provide the higher-level pool and cooperative cancellation policy.

            Why is Java volatile not a direct replacement for C++ atomics?

            The memory and synchronization rules differ between the languages. C++ data-race safety requires a valid atomic or locking protocol; the keyword alone is not enough.

            What should you verify before translating a concurrency API?

            Its ownership, memory-ordering, wake-up, cancellation, exception, and lifetime guarantees—not only the method names.

            APPENDIX
            C
            A message-passing framework and complete ATM example · printed pp. 342–359

            Give each actor its own state, then let typed messages coordinate the work.

            This is the book’s next section after Appendix B—not a numbered chapter. It completes the earlier message-passing example with a small C++11 mailbox framework and three cooperating actors: an ATM, a bank, and the user interface.

            CMessage framework DesignTyped messages ExampleATM state machine Try itATM simulator ReviewSummary & recall
            Scope note · an architectural study aid, not a production banking system.

            The simulator uses a fixed demo account, PIN 1937, and starting balance of 199 units. It visualizes message routing deterministically; it does not model actual threads, a network, real authentication, or secure payment processing.

            Framework
            A mailbox boundary keeps receivers in control

            Senders can post; receivers own their inbox and decide what to handle.

            The book’s framework type-erases messages behind a base class, queues them under a mutex, and blocks on a condition variable until an item arrives. A lightweight sender shares access to posting without exposing the receiving side.

            Mailbox

            Queue typed envelopes.

            A wrapper stores one concrete message type behind a common base pointer. The receiver can take the next envelope without knowing its type yet.

            Sender

            Share only the post capability.

            A sender is a small handle to a queue. Requests can carry a reply sender so the recipient knows where to answer.

            Receiver

            Own the queue and wait for work.

            The receiving actor blocks on a predicate wait, pops one message, and processes it in its own thread.

            Dispatcher

            Route a message to a typed handler.

            A handler chain checks the envelope type and invokes the matching callable. Unmatched messages can be offered to the next handler.

            InterfaceInput / displayPosts button events; displays replies
            →
            ATM actorOwn state machinePIN, current state, chosen action
            →
            Bank actorAccount stateChecks PIN, balance, withdrawal
            Replies travel back through sender handles; the ATM then posts display or cash-output messages.
            C++11 · a compact typed-mailbox sketch
            Adapted teaching example; one blocking consumer
            #include <condition_variable>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>

struct message_base
{
    virtual ~message_base() {}
};

template<class M>
struct envelope : message_base
{
    M value;
    explicit envelope(M value_) : value(std::move(value_)) {}
};

class mailbox
{
    std::mutex mutex_;
    std::condition_variable ready_;
    std::queue<std::shared_ptr<message_base> > messages_;
public:
    template<class M>
    void post(M message)
    {
        std::shared_ptr<message_base> boxed =
            std::make_shared<envelope<M> >(std::move(message));
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
            messages_.push(std::move(boxed));
        }
        ready_.notify_one();
    }

    std::shared_ptr<message_base> wait_and_pop()
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
        ready_.wait(lock, [this] { return !messages_.empty(); });
        auto next = messages_.front();
        messages_.pop();
        return next;
    }
};
            The envelope makes the queue heterogeneous while the mutex protects only the queue structure. A receiver can use dynamic_cast or a tagged visitor to recover the concrete type; a production design should also define shutdown, error handling, and back-pressure.
            Messages
            Requests, replies, and local state

            Messages describe events; actors own the mutable state behind them.

            Keep each message small and explicit. A request that needs a reply can carry the requesting actor’s sender handle; the receiver answers by posting a distinct reply message.

            Interface → ATM

            Events

            card_inserted, digit_pressed, withdraw_pressed, balance_pressed, and cancel_pressed.

            ATM → Bank

            Requests

            verify_pin, withdraw, and get_balance. A reply sender identifies the ATM’s inbox.

            Bank → ATM

            Replies

            pin_verified/pin_incorrect, withdraw_ok/withdraw_denied, and a balance value.

            ATM → Interface

            Effects

            Display prompts and errors, eject the card, or issue cash only after the bank has approved the withdrawal.

            Why actors help.

            The ATM thread owns its PIN and state-machine position; the bank thread owns the balance. They exchange messages rather than concurrently mutating one another’s data. The message queue still needs synchronization, but the business state has a clear owner.

            Framework caveat from the book example.

            The original dispatcher performs blocking dispatch from a destructor and uses a close_queue exception to stop the loop. That illustrates the message flow, but throwing from destructors is unusual and fragile; do not copy that shutdown mechanism into production code unchanged.

            ATM
            A finite-state machine driven by messages

            Only the messages valid for the current state advance the workflow.

            The ATM transitions from card entry to PIN verification, then to an action. Replies and button events choose the next transition; a successful withdrawal reports the completed transaction before the card is ejected.

            01

            Waiting for card

            card_inserted stores the account and requests a PIN.

            02

            Entering / verifying PIN

            Four digit messages form a PIN request. The bank replies verified or incorrect.

            03

            Waiting for an action

            Ask for a balance, request a fixed withdrawal, or cancel.

            04

            Complete and return

            Show the result, issue approved cash, eject the card, then await another card.

            RequestATM → Bankwithdraw(account, amount, reply-sender)
            →
            DecisionBank owns balanceapprove or deny; update balance once
            →
            Reply / effectBank → ATM → Interfacereply, display result, then eject

            Appendix C · study summary

            Make the mailbox the boundary and the message the contract.

            The complete example combines a blocking typed queue, send-only handles, dispatch, three actor-owned state machines, and an explicit shutdown path.

            • Use distinct message types for input events, requests, replies, and output effects.
            • Keep mutable actor state private to its owning thread; route work through a mailbox.
            • Carry a reply sender when a request must return a result to the original actor.
            • Define how queues close and how all actor threads join; a wake-up is part of the protocol.
            • Treat the book’s dispatcher as a teaching example, not a production exception-handling template.

            Appendix C quick recall

            Try to answer before opening each note.

            What does the receiver own that a sender does not?

            The receiver owns the message queue and can wait for and remove messages. A sender is a posting handle that can be copied and passed to other actors.

            Why include a sender in a request message?

            It tells the recipient where to post a reply without giving that recipient direct access to the requester’s internal state.

            Why separate the ATM, bank, and interface into actors?

            Each actor owns its own state and processes one mailbox message at a time. That reduces shared mutable state and makes transitions easier to reason about.

            Is the simulator a real concurrent banking system?

            No. It deterministically illustrates message ordering and state transitions. It has no real threads, secure authentication, durable accounts, or payment processing.

The mailbox code sketch and ATM simulator are original study aids; the shutdown caveat distinguishes the book’s demonstration framework from production guidance.
