            D
            C++ Thread Library reference · printed pp. 360–486

            Choose the library tool by the guarantee you need.

            This appendix is a compact map of the C++11 concurrency library: clocks, condition variables, atomics, futures, locks, compile-time ratios, and threads. Use it to find the right family, then check the exact contract for the operation you need.

            Start hereChoose by task D.1 · chronoDurations & clocks D.2 · condition_variableWait on a predicate D.3 · atomicAtomic operations D.4 · futureResults & tasks D.5 · mutexProtect shared state D.6 · ratioCompile-time units D.7 · threadStart & join workers ReviewQuick recall
            Scope · a C++11-era field reference, not a verbatim or normative copy.

            The source appendix documents the C++11 thread library. This study map emphasizes practical selection and safety rules; it does not cover later additions such as jthread, stop tokens, barriers, or semaphores. Check the C++ standard and your implementation’s documentation for the exact version you target.

            Choose
            A small API compass

            Start with the job, not with a familiar class name.

            Select a task to get a suggested C++11 facility and its main caution. The linked cards below summarize each header.

            Recommendation · <chrono>

            Use std::chrono::steady_clock.

            Capture a start and end time point from the same steady clock, then subtract them to get a duration.

            Watch for: system_clock is wall time and can move; high_resolution_clock is not guaranteed to be steady.

            Open the chrono reference ↓
            D.1–D.7
            Header-by-header quick reference

            Seven headers cover time, waiting, atomicity, results, locking, units, and workers.

            Use these as entry points. The guarantees come from the operation and its preconditions—not just from the type’s name.

            D.1<chrono>

            Represent elapsed time with durations and clock-specific time points.

            Core vocabulary

            duration<Rep, Period>, time_point<Clock, Duration>, duration_cast, and Clock::now().

            Pick the clock

            steady_clock is guaranteed steady; system_clock is adjustable wall time; high_resolution_clock may be an alias for either.

            Rule: use a steady clock for elapsed time and deadlines. Converting to a coarser integral duration can truncate.

            Connects to Chapter 4 · timed waits
            D.2<condition_variable>

            Block until shared state may have changed.

            Core operations

            wait, wait_for, wait_until, notify_one, and notify_all.

            Choose the lock type

            condition_variable works with unique_lock<mutex>; condition_variable_any accepts other lock types.

            Rule: wait with a predicate protected by the same mutex. Spurious wakeups are allowed; notifications are not stored events.

            Connects to Chapter 3 · shared state
            D.3<atomic>

            Make individual operations on a value atomic.

            Core types and operations

            atomic<T>, guaranteed-lock-free atomic_flag, load, store, exchange, read-modify-write operations, compare/exchange, atomic_thread_fence, and atomic_signal_fence. Check is_lock_free() when it matters.

            Memory-order vocabulary

            The default is seq_cst; relaxed gives atomicity only. Release/acquire can publish data when the acquire observes the release (or its release sequence).

            Rule: atomic does not mean lock-free or make a multi-variable invariant atomic. A weak compare/exchange may fail spuriously.

            Connects to Chapter 5 · memory ordering
            D.4<future>

            Transport a result or exception from an operation.

            Pick the abstraction

            future for one consumer; shared_future for shared reads; promise for explicit fulfillment; packaged_task to wrap a callable.

            Launch policy matters

            async can run asynchronously or be deferred when using its default policy. std::launch::async requests asynchronous execution.

            Rule: future::get() retrieves the result and invalidates that future; exceptions from the work are rethrown by get().

            Connects to Chapter 4 · futures
            D.5<mutex>

            Guard a shared invariant with scoped ownership of a lock.

            Core types

            mutex, timed and recursive variants, lock_guard, and the movable unique_lock.

            Coordination helpers

            lock/try_lock coordinate multiple mutexes; once_flag and call_once perform one-time initialization.

            Rule: prefer RAII. Use unique_lock when a condition variable must unlock/relock; use std::lock to acquire several mutexes together.

            Connects to Chapter 6 · locking
            D.6<ratio>

            Describe and combine rational constants at compile time.

            Core vocabulary

            ratio<Num, Den> stores a normalized rational value; aliases such as milli and micro describe common scales.

            Where it appears

            Duration periods use ratios, so duration<int, milli> represents milliseconds. Ratio arithmetic and comparisons are compile-time operations.

            Rule: ratio is a unit/scale metaprogramming tool, not a runtime clock or a substitute for dimensional design.

            Connects to D.1 · chrono durations
            D.7<thread>

            Start a worker and explicitly decide how it ends.

            Core operations

            thread, join, detach, joinable, get_id, and the this_thread namespace.

            Current-thread helpers

            yield, sleep_for, sleep_until, and get_id. Sleep may last longer than requested.

            Rule: a thread object must be joined or detached before destruction; destroying a still-joinable thread calls std::terminate.

            Connects to Chapter 2 · thread lifetime
            Recipes
            C++11 composition patterns

            Combine the primitives around a clear state predicate.

            A condition variable does not carry the condition: the mutex protects the state, and the predicate decides whether the waiter can proceed.

            C++11 · predicate-based timed wait
            D.1 + D.2 · steady deadline, mutex-protected state
            #include <chrono>
#include <condition_variable>
#include <mutex>

void publish_ready(std::mutex& mutex,
                   std::condition_variable& changed,
                   bool& ready)
{
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex);
        ready = true;
    }
    changed.notify_one();
}

bool wait_until_ready(std::mutex& mutex,
                      std::condition_variable& changed,
                      bool& ready)
{
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mutex);
    const auto deadline = std::chrono::steady_clock::now()
                        + std::chrono::seconds(2);
    return changed.wait_until(lock, deadline, [&ready]
    {
        return ready;
    });
}
            The caller must set ready while holding the same mutex, then notify. The predicate overload rechecks state after wakeups and returns false only when the deadline expires while the predicate remains false.
            D.3atomic counter
            #include <atomic>

int main()
{
    std::atomic<unsigned> completed{0};
    completed.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    return completed.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == 1 ? 0 : 1;
}

            Relaxed ordering is suitable for an independent count when it does not publish other data. Choose stronger ordering only to express a real synchronization relationship.

            D.4async result
            #include <future>

int main()
{
    std::future<int> answer =
        std::async(std::launch::async, [] { return 42; });
    return answer.get() == 42 ? 0 : 1;
}

            Explicit launch policy avoids the default policy’s deferred-or-asynchronous choice. Store the future and retrieve the result once.

            Three easy-to-miss library contracts
            • wait_for is not a predicate: loop on the state yourself, or use its predicate overload so spurious wakeups do not become false success.
            • hardware_concurrency() is only a hint and may return zero; do not treat it as an exact worker-pool size.
            • Exceptions escaping a thread’s top-level callable call std::terminate; catch inside the worker or transport the exception with a future.
            Appendix D · study summary

            Choose the primitive that matches the coordination contract.

            Measure with clocks, wait on protected predicates, publish results through futures, and keep each thread’s lifetime explicit.

            • Use steady_clock for durations and deadlines; reserve system_clock for wall-clock timestamps.
            • Protect condition state with a mutex and always wait using a predicate.
            • Use atomics for independent atomic operations; use a mutex for multi-step invariants.
            • Know whether a future is single-consumer, shared, explicitly fulfilled, or launched with a deferred policy.
            • Acquire locks with RAII and join or intentionally detach every thread before its owner is destroyed.

            Appendix D quick recall

            Try to answer before opening each note.

            Which clock should you use to measure elapsed time?

            std::chrono::steady_clock: it is guaranteed not to move backward. Use system_clock when you need wall-clock time, and do not assume high_resolution_clock is steady.

            Why should condition-variable waits use a predicate?

            Wakeups may be spurious, and notifications do not store a condition. The predicate rechecks mutex-protected state and keeps waiting until that state is true or a timed wait expires.

            What is the difference between future and shared_future?

            A future is a single-consumer result handle; get() consumes its shared state. A shared_future permits multiple reads of the result.

            What happens if a joinable std::thread is destroyed?

            The program calls std::terminate. Arrange a join or an intentional detach before the thread object’s destructor runs.

            ↗Source: Anthony Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action: Practical Multithreading, Appendix D, “C++ Thread Library reference,” printed pp. 360–486. This page is an original condensed study guide; it is not a replacement for the C++ standard or current library documentation.
